evidence.snippet: EA/TEF is a component of the VACTERL association, which includes vertebral, anal, cardiovascular, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies, and is seen in 10% to 30% of EA/TEF patients [1, 19].
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports VACTERL association as a frequent associated context in EA/TEF.

evidence.snippet: About 10% of patients with CHARGE syndrome display EA/TEF.
evidence.explanation: This review supports EA/TEF as a feature in a subset of CHARGE syndrome patients.

evidence.snippet: caused by mutations in the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding (CHD7) gene
evidence.explanation: This supports CHD7 as the gene underlying the relevant syndromic association.

evidence.snippet: Feingold syndrome is caused by germline mutations in, or deletions of, the MYCN gene on chromosome 2p24.1.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies MYCN as the causal gene for the Feingold syndrome association.

evidence.snippet: About 30% to 40% of patients diagnosed with Feingold syndrome have EA/TEF [25].
evidence.explanation: This review directly supports EA/TEF enrichment in Feingold syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Deletions and mutations of the SOX2 gene are causative for the phenotype of clinical anophthalmia/optic nerve hypoplasia, esophageal atresia, and/or genital anomalies in the AEG syndrome [28].
evidence.explanation: This review directly links SOX2 alterations to a syndromic phenotype including esophageal atresia.

evidence.snippet: mutations in the FOXF1 gene, in patients with alveolar capillary dysplasia combined with VACTERL-associated anomalies, including EA/TEF [24••].
evidence.explanation: This review links FOXF1-region alterations to human VACTERL-associated anomalies including EA/TEF.

evidence.snippet: Genes of developmental pathways are involved, including vitamin A effectors (Rarα, Rarβ), effectors of the sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway (Shh, Gli2, Gli3, Foxf1)
evidence.explanation: This supports FOXF1 and SHH-pathway effectors as model-organism developmental susceptibility genes for tracheoesophageal anomalies.

evidence.snippet: EA is treated surgically to restore the oesophageal interruption and, if present, ligate and divide the TEF.
evidence.explanation: The disease primer directly states the surgical repair goals.

evidence.snippet: surgical repair of their defect defined as esophageal reconstruction with or without ligation of TEF
evidence.explanation: The surgical cohort defines repair as esophageal reconstruction with or without TEF ligation.

treatments/0.description: Standard neonatal management restores esophageal continuity and ligates or divides a tracheoesophageal fistula when present.

evidence.snippet: Questions on the diagnosis, and treatment of gastroesophageal reflux
evidence.explanation: The guideline explicitly covers treatment of GERD in children with EA/TEF.

treatments/1.description: Long-term care includes treatment of gastroesophageal reflux after EA/TEF repair.

evidence.snippet: These strictures are often treated by balloon dilatation (BD) and currently balloon dilatation (fluoroscopic or endoscopic) is the preferred primary treatment method.
evidence.explanation: This systematic review directly supports balloon dilatation for anastomotic strictures after EA repair.

treatments/2.description: Anastomotic strictures after esophageal atresia repair are often managed with fluoroscopic or endoscopic balloon dilatation.

evidence.snippet: We identified a chimeric transcript that is expressed in FL-HCC but not in adjacent normal liver and that arises as the result of a ~400-kilobase deletion on chromosome 19.
evidence.explanation: The founding observation defining this node - the deletion, its size, and its tumour restriction.

evidence.snippet: Evidence supporting the presence of the DNAJB1-PRKACA chimeric transcript in 100% of the FL-HCCs examined (15/15) suggests that this genetic alteration contributes to tumor pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the near-universal recurrence on which this entry's single-driver framing rests.

evidence.snippet: There are relatively few coding, somatic mutations in this cancer, putting it on the low end of the mutational spectrum.
evidence.explanation: Whole-genome evidence for the low mutational burden that makes this lesion interpretable as the driver rather than one of many.

steps/1.description: A somatic heterozygous deletion of roughly 400 kb on chromosome 19 joins DNAJB1 in frame to PRKACA. The deletion is present in essentially every fibrolamellar carcinoma and in no adjacent normal liver, and whole-genome sequencing finds no recurrent second structural event alongside it.

evidence.snippet: The chimeric RNA is predicted to code for a protein containing the amino-terminal domain of DNAJB1, a homolog of the molecular chaperone DNAJ, fused in frame with PRKACA, the catalytic domain of protein kinase A.
evidence.explanation: Describes the domain architecture of the chimera this node names.

evidence.snippet: DNAJB1-PRKACA was expressed 10-fold higher than the wild-type PRKACA transcript, resulting in overexpression of the mutant protein in tumors.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the expression imbalance between mutant and wild-type kinase.

steps/2.description: The chimera carries the DNAJB1 amino-terminal chaperone-binding domain fused to the PRKACA catalytic domain. Its transcript is expressed about tenfold above wild-type PRKACA, so the tumour cell holds far more of the mutant kinase than of the normal one.

evidence.snippet: Consequently, FL-HCCs possess elevated cAMP-stimulated PKA activity compared to normal livers, despite similar Kms between the mutant and wild-type kinases.
evidence.explanation: States both the elevated activity and the Km comparison that locates the cause in abundance rather than in altered catalysis.

steps/3.description: Tumours show higher cAMP-stimulated PKA catalytic activity than normal liver. The mutant and wild-type kinases have similar Km values, so the excess activity is a consequence of how much mutant kinase is present rather than of a changed affinity for substrate.

evidence.snippet: a unique property of this fusion enzyme is the ability to recruit heat shock protein 70 (Hsp70)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the acquired, wild-type-absent property this node describes.

evidence.snippet: The J-domain also alters several biochemical properties of the RIIβ holoenzyme: It is easier to activate with cAMP, and the cooperativity is reduced.
evidence.explanation: A measured consequence of the retained J-domain, independent of the Hsp70 result: the same domain that recruits Hsp70 also changes how the holoenzyme responds to cAMP. Graded IN_VITRO - the paper is a cryo-EM and small-angle-scattering study of purified holoenzyme, with molecular dynamics as one component rather than the whole method.

steps/4.description: The retained DNAJ domain lets the fusion recruit Hsp70, a property wild-type PKA does not have. A-kinase anchoring protein Lbc, itself upregulated in these tumours, clusters the resulting DNAJ-PKAc/Hsp70 subcomplexes with a RAF-MEK-ERK module, so the fusion does not simply signal harder - it assembles a signalling complex the normal kinase never forms. This is the clearest evidence that the lesion is neomorphic rather than merely activating.

evidence.snippet: Phosphoproteomic profiling demonstrates that DNAJ-PKAc biases the signaling landscape toward ERK activation and engages downstream kinase cascades.
evidence.explanation: Direct phosphoproteomic evidence for the ERK bias this node asserts.

steps/5.description: Phosphoproteomic profiling shows the fusion shifts the cell's signalling landscape toward ERK activation and engages downstream kinase cascades.

evidence.snippet: DNAJB1-PRKACA inactivates the SIK tumor suppressors in patient-derived FLC cells and engineered models.
evidence.explanation: The inactivation event this node records, shown in both patient-derived cells and engineered models.

steps/6.description: The fusion kinase inactivates the salt-inducible kinases, which act as tumour suppressors in this setting. This is the phosphorylation event itself, separate from the transcriptional consequence it releases.

evidence.snippet: DNAJB1-PRKACA-mediated inactivation of the SIK stimulates CRTC2-p300-mediated transcription to drive tumor growth.
evidence.explanation: Names the coactivator complex and connects it to growth, which is the claim this node carries.

steps/7.description: With SIK activity lost, the CRTC2 coactivator and the p300 acetyltransferase drive a transcriptional program that supports tumour growth. This arm was defined in 2024 by combining model systems with human tumour specimens.

evidence.snippet: Two signaling networks were identified downstream of PKA: RAS/MAPK components and an Aurora Kinase A (AURKA)/glycogen synthase kinase (GSK3) sub-network with activity toward MYC oncoproteins.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the AURKA/GSK3 sub-network this node names.

evidence.snippet: Expression of several known oncogenes, such as ErbB2 and Aurora Kinase A, was increased in tumor samples.
evidence.explanation: Independent transcriptomic confirmation that Aurora kinase A is raised in human tumours.

evidence.snippet: The associated DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion transcript RNA codes for the catalytic domain of protein kinase A and overexpression of Aurora kinase A (AURKA).
evidence.explanation: The trial report's own statement of the rationale, which is how this node became a drug target rather than only a phosphoproteomic observation.

steps/8.description: Phosphoproteomics across PKA-activating lesions identifies an Aurora kinase A / GSK3 sub-network as one of two conserved signalling outputs downstream of the fusion. Aurora kinase A is also raised in human tumours by transcriptomics, and it is the target that took the first fusion-rationalised drug into a trial in this disease.

evidence.snippet: the primary mechanism of PKA effects on MYC in our cell models was translation and could be blocked with the eIF4A inhibitor zotatifin
evidence.explanation: Establishes both that MYC protein rises and that the route is translational, which is the specific claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: This compound dramatically reduced c-MYC expression and inhibited FLC cell line growth in vitro.
evidence.explanation: The pharmacological test in a fibrolamellar carcinoma line, which is what ties this node to growth rather than leaving it a signalling observation.

steps/9.description: c-MYC protein rises in fibrolamellar carcinoma cells. The dominant route is translational rather than transcriptional: blocking translation initiation with an eIF4A inhibitor collapsed MYC expression and cell growth, which is the observation that separates this node from a transcriptional MYC amplification.

evidence.snippet: Tumorigenesis was significantly enhanced by genetic activation of β-catenin, an observation supported by evidence of recurrent Wnt pathway mutations in human FL-HCC
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the mouse cooperation effect and its human genomic correlate, which is what this node claims.

steps/10.description: The fusion kinase interacts with beta-catenin, and activating beta-catenin genetically markedly increases tumour formation in mouse models. Recurrent Wnt pathway mutations in human tumours support this as a real cooperating route. It is curated as cooperation, not as a second required driver - the fusion alone suffices.

evidence.snippet: Fibrolamellar carcinoma and adenomyomatosis samples presented increased expression of Aurora kinase A, c-MYC, and ornithine decarboxylase when compared to normal liver, while ornithine transcarbamylase was decreased.
evidence.explanation: Measures every enzyme in the proposed chain in human tumour tissue, which is what this node records.

steps/11.description: Tumour tissue shows raised Aurora kinase A, c-MYC and ornithine decarboxylase with reduced ornithine transcarbamylase. Suppressing a urea cycle enzyme is how a liver tumour comes to phenocopy an inborn error of metabolism.

evidence.snippet: Livers from 12 of the 15 mice given the vectors to induce the Dnajb1-Prkaca gene fusion, but none of the 11 mice given the control vector, developed neoplasms.
evidence.explanation: The sufficiency experiment, with its control arm, that makes this node a demonstrated consequence rather than an inferred one.

evidence.snippet: overexpression of the wild-type PRKACA was unable to fully recapitulate the oncogenic activity of DNAJB1-PRKACA, implying that FL-HCC does not simply result from enhanced PRKACA expression
evidence.explanation: The negative control that distinguishes a neomorphic fusion from simple PKA overactivity - the entry's central mechanistic claim.

steps/12.description: The convergent consequence is transformation of hepatocytes in a liver with no underlying disease. The fusion is sufficient on its own: engineering it into adult mouse liver, with no other engineered alteration and no carcinogen exposure, produces tumours resembling human fibrolamellar carcinoma, while overexpressing wild-type PRKACA does not.

steps/13.description: Parallel bands of collagen encircle nests of tumour cells, producing the architecture the disease is named for. This is a tumour-induced stroma distinct from cirrhotic fibrosis, and the tumour arises in a liver that is not otherwise fibrotic. The cellular route from transformed hepatocyte to lamellar collagen is not established, so it is modelled as an edge with unknown intermediates rather than asserted.

evidence.snippet: Patients typically lack cirrhosis or other risk factors and present with a large tumor burden and locally invasive or metastatic disease
evidence.explanation: States both the absent-risk-factor context and the advanced stage at presentation.

steps/14.description: A large liver mass in a patient with no cirrhosis and none of the risk factors that precede conventional hepatocellular carcinoma. Because the symptoms are nonspecific and the patients are young and otherwise well, a substantial fraction present with a large tumour burden and locally invasive or metastatic disease.

steps/15.description: A paraneoplastic encephalopathy driven by the tumour's own suppression of urea cycle capacity rather than by liver failure. It is the reason a fibrolamellar carcinoma patient can present looking like a urea cycle disorder while their non-tumour liver function is preserved.

evidence.snippet: Immunoprecipitation and Western blot analyses confirmed that the chimeric protein is expressed in tumor tissue, and a cell culture assay indicated that it retains kinase activity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the deletion yields an expressed, catalytically active protein rather than only a transcript, which is what this edge claims.

edges/1.description: The fusion transcript is translated into a chimeric protein that is detectable in tumour tissue and retains kinase activity.

evidence.snippet: the proto-oncogene A-kinase anchoring protein-Lbc is up-regulated in FLC and functions to cluster DNAJ-PKAc/Hsp70 sub-complexes with a RAF-MEK-ERK kinase module
evidence.explanation: Names the scaffolding step that connects this node to ERK activation.

edges/6.description: Clustering the fusion with a RAF-MEK-ERK module is what redirects the cell's signalling output toward ERK.

evidence.snippet: DNAJB1-PRKACA-mediated inactivation of the SIK stimulates CRTC2-p300-mediated transcription to drive tumor growth.
evidence.explanation: Gives the ordering of the two steps, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/8.description: Losing SIK activity is what releases the CRTC2-p300 coactivator complex; the source states the two steps in that order.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that Aurora Kinase A (AURKA), glycogen synthase kinase (GSK)–3B and the eukaryotic Initiation Factor (eIF)–4B all link PKA and c-MYC
evidence.explanation: States the link between the kinases in this node and c-MYC, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/10.description: The sub-network was identified by its activity toward MYC oncoproteins; the intermediate steps between the kinases and the protein pool are partly mapped and partly not.

evidence.snippet: An ornithine transcarboxylase dysfunction was suggested as a result of increased ornithine decarboxylase activity induced by c-Myc overexpression.
evidence.explanation: States the proposed c-Myc to ODC to OTC route this edge represents. Quoted as the source frames it, as a proposal rather than a settled fact.

edges/12.description: Raised c-Myc is the proposed driver of the ornithine decarboxylase increase that in turn suppresses ornithine transcarbamylase.

edges/14.description: The tumour induces its characteristic stroma, but the steps between transformation and lamellar collagen deposition are not established.

evidence.snippet: Evidence supporting the presence of the DNAJB1-PRKACA chimeric transcript in 100% of the FL-HCCs examined (15/15) suggests that this genetic alteration contributes to tumor pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The founding recurrence figure.

evidence.snippet: The lack of a second-hit mutation in the genomic landscape of fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma makes the DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion protein the best target for diagnostic and therapeutic advancements.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the absence of a recurrent cooperating lesion, which is why this entry treats the fusion as the driver rather than one of several.

genes/0.notes: Curated as a structural fusion rather than a sequence variant. `gene_term` carries PRKACA because the slot is single-valued and the catalytic activity resides there; DNAJB1 (hgnc:5270) contributes the amino-terminal chaperone-binding domain and is bound on the pathophysiology node.

evidence.snippet: Patients who were not treated with surgical intervention had about 3 times increased risk for death (HR 2.8, 95% CI 1.68-4.72, P = 0.000).
evidence.explanation: The population-based effect estimate this treatment rests on.

treatments/0.description: Hepatectomy is the mainstay and the only modality with a demonstrated survival effect in population data. Patients not treated surgically had roughly three times the risk of death.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Resection removes the tumour bulk; because the background liver is not cirrhotic, more of it can be taken than in conventional hepatocellular carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: Radiation and chemotherapy did not significantly affect outcomes.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE because it contradicts the claim that this treatment benefits patients. The same sentence covers radiation.

evidence.snippet: There are no standard treatments for advanced FLC, and clinical trials with targeted, conventional, and immune therapies have shown limited benefit.
evidence.explanation: Supports the description's claim that no systemic option is established, across drug classes rather than only cytotoxics.

treatments/1.description: Curated as a treatment that does not work. Chemotherapy is given to nearly half of patients in population data yet has no measurable effect on outcome, and the tumours were described as poorly chemoresponsive from the founding report onward. Recording the negative result is the point.

evidence.snippet: fusion breakpoint occurs within an intron, making the sequence of the chimera consistent across patients. This allows a single vaccine to be broadly applicable for patients with FLC.
evidence.explanation: States why a single shared peptide works for this disease - the intronic breakpoint makes the chimera's sequence identical across patients.

evidence.snippet: DNAJ-PKAc-specific T cell responses were detected in 9 of 12 patients after treatment.
evidence.explanation: The immunological primary endpoint, which is what a phase 1 trial is powered for.

evidence.snippet: In the subset of patients who completed the initial priming phase the disease control rate was 75% (9/12), with three partial responses (25%).
evidence.explanation: The clinical signal, quoted with its own denominator. Curated as an early-phase observation, not as an efficacy claim.

evidence.snippet: Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events were reported by six patients (37.5%).
evidence.explanation: The toxicity result, recorded alongside the response figures rather than omitted.

treatments/2.description: A synthetic long peptide spanning the fusion breakpoint, given with a poly-ICLC adjuvant and dual checkpoint blockade. This is the therapeutic payoff of the entry's single-driver framing: because the breakpoint falls inside an intron, the chimeric junction sequence is the same in every patient, so one off-the-shelf peptide is a shared neoantigen for the whole disease. Phase 1 only - the disease control figure comes from 12 evaluable patients and is not an efficacy result.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: The immunogen is the chimeric junction itself, so the treatment targets the driver lesion directly rather than a downstream consequence of it.

evidence.snippet: A systematic review of 35 series involving 575 patients indicated a 5-year survival rate ranging from 29% to 55% for those undergoing liver transplantation
evidence.explanation: The pooled survival range across 35 series. Quoted as a range rather than a point estimate because that is how the source reports it.

evidence.snippet: Our patient, with poor prognostic criteria such as hilar lymph node metastasis, microvascular invasion, and poor differentiation, had 22 months of tumor-free survival and 26 months of overall survival after having undergone living-donor liver transplant.
evidence.explanation: A single case, curated for what it shows about the limits of the procedure: hilar nodal metastasis and microvascular invasion were present and the patient died at 26 months. One case is weak evidence and is recorded as such.

treatments/3.description: Considered for liver-confined disease that cannot be resected. Reported five-year survival spans a wide range across series, and the individual reports make clear that nodal and vascular involvement drive the outcome rather than the transplant itself.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Total hepatectomy with grafting removes tumour that partial resection cannot clear, at the cost of lifelong immunosuppression.

evidence.snippet: FLC was an independent risk factor for LN positivity, suggesting a role for routine LN sampling in these patients.
evidence.explanation: The staging rationale: this histology is itself a predictor of positive nodes, which is the study's argument for sampling.

evidence.snippet: In AYA patients with HCC, LN sampling was not associated with an independent survival benefit.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against a survival-benefit claim, which the deep-research report asserted and this cohort does not support. The same paper supplies both items because it makes both findings.

treatments/4.description: Curated because the evidence points two ways and both directions matter. Fibrolamellar histology independently predicts node positivity, so sampling is informative for staging; but in the same cohort, sampling itself carried no independent survival benefit. This entry records the staging rationale and the absent survival effect as separate evidence items rather than resolving them into a recommendation.

evidence.snippet: The limited results, one patient (3%) with a partial response and 57% of patients with stable disease, do not support further evaluation of ENMD-2076 as single agent.
evidence.explanation: Graded REFUTE against the claim that this treatment benefits patients. The response and stable-disease figures are quoted with the trial's own conclusion attached to them.

evidence.snippet: The study provided no rationale for further studying ENMD-2076 as a single agent in FLC.
evidence.explanation: The trial's formal conclusion, quoted separately from the numbers behind it.

treatments/5.description: ENMD-2076, an oral Aurora A inhibitor, was the first drug taken into a trial on the strength of this entry's own mechanism - AURKA overexpression downstream of the fusion. It is curated because it did not work. A single partial response in 35 patients is the counterexample to reading a phosphoproteomic node as a validated drug target.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: The drug targets Aurora kinase A, which is the node's own gene product.

open_questions/0.rationale: The lamellar stroma is the tumour's defining histologic feature and the origin of its name, yet the entry cannot connect it to the driver. TGF-beta overexpression is the proposed route in the literature, but the support is correlative and histological rather than a demonstrated causal chain, so the edge from transformation to stroma is curated with unknown intermediates and no evidence attached. The gap matters because the fibrosis is not cirrhotic and the surrounding liver is normal, so whatever drives it is tumour-directed rather than a background process.

open_questions/1.rationale: MONDO places MONDO:0006210 under hepatocellular carcinoma, and this entry's `parents` follows it. The evidence curated here points the other way: the genomic landscape is distinct, the driver is absent from conventional hepatocellular carcinoma and from every other liver tumour tested, the patient population and risk-factor profile do not overlap, and the published sequencing describes it as "a distinct carcinoma". The entry does not attempt to resolve the ontology question - it uses MONDO's term and hierarchy as given, curates the evidence that bears on the placement, and records the disagreement here rather than silently asserting either answer.

evidence.snippet: 900 genes have been identified as monogenic causes of DEEs and many cell components and processes
evidence.explanation: Establishes the extreme monogenic heterogeneity of the DEE umbrella, the defining upstream trigger of this entry.

evidence.snippet: Genetic DEEs have been associated with mutations in many genes involved in different functions including cell migration, proliferation, and organization, neuronal excitability, and synapse transmission and plasticity.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the functional gene classes affected, matching the ion-channel, synaptic, and neurodevelopmental categories described in this node.

steps/56.description:
A de novo or inherited pathogenic variant in one of a large and growing set of genes encoding voltage-gated ion channels (e.g. SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNA2, KCNT1, CACNA1E, HCN1), presynaptic vesicle-cycle and neurotransmitter-release machinery (STXBP1, DNM1, SNAP25, CPLX1, UNC13A), postsynaptic glutamate or GABA receptors (GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, GABRA1, GABRB3), or chromatin/transcriptional regulators active in neurodevelopment (CDKL5, FOXG1, CHD2) disrupts normal neuronal excitability or synaptic signaling.
Gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry, beyond the examples above, are CACNA2D1 (the alpha-2-delta-1 auxiliary subunit of CaV1 and CaV2 voltage-gated calcium channels), FGF13/FHF2 (an intracellular regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels), SV2A (a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein and the binding site of levetiracetam), FRRS1L (an AMPA receptor outer-core protein), LGI1 together with its postsynaptic receptor ADAM22, BAIAP2 (dendritic spine morphogenesis and excitatory synapse formation), and ACTL6B (a subunit of the neuron-specific chromatin remodelling complex nBAF). Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row.
The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with four further voltage-gated channel subunits (SCN3A/Nav1.3, KCNC2/Kv3.2, KCNH5/EAG2-Kv10.2, and the sodium-activated potassium channel KCNT2); the stretch-activated channel TMEM63B; four GABA receptor subunits, namely the GABA-A subunits GABRB2, GABRA2 and GABRA5 together with the metabotropic GABA-B subunit GABBR2; the vesicular GABA transporter SLC32A1; and three further components of the presynaptic vesicle cycle, namely the AAA ATPase NSF, which acts in SNARE complex assembly and disassembly, its beta attachment protein NAPB, and the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1.

evidence.snippet: many other mechanisms have been identified: impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders, disruption of dendrite and axon growth, maintenance and synapse formation abnormalities -synaptopathies.
evidence.explanation: Names the non-channelopathy mechanism classes that this node collects, in the review the entry already uses for the two-component DEE model.

evidence.snippet: Genetic DEEs have been associated with mutations in many genes involved in different functions including cell migration, proliferation, and organization, neuronal excitability, and synapse transmission and plasticity.
evidence.explanation: Supports the breadth of gene functions represented at this node, including cell migration and organization.

steps/57.description: A large share of the genes in which pathogenic variants cause genetic DEE encode neither an ion channel nor a core synaptic protein, and the DEE literature explicitly separates these mechanisms from the channelopathies. The gene-defined subtypes wired at this node in this entry span Rac-GEF-dependent neuronal polarity (DOCK7), actin and protein-phosphatase-1 regulation in cortical migration (PHACTR1), receptor tyrosine kinase signalling (NTRK2), spliceosomal small nuclear RNA (RNU2-2), de-UFMylation (UFSP2), endoplasmic-reticulum stress signalling (RNF13), mitochondrial protein biosynthesis and mitochondrial trafficking (PARS2, TRAK1), purine metabolism and asparagine-linked glycosylation (ITPA, ALG13), endolysosomal acidification (ATP6V0A1), Na+/K+-ATPase pump function and neutral amino-acid transport (ATP1A2, SLC38A3), DNA repair (PNKP), and one gene in the 1q41-q42 microdeletion interval whose molecular function no reference cited here states (FBXO28). The DEE-series subtypes added under this parent extend that list with a Krebs cycle enzyme (MDH2), an endoplasmic-reticulum co-chaperone (CNPY3), a cut homeodomain transcription factor (CUX2), a cohesin subunit (SMC1A), a factor that targets arginine tRNAs for 3-methylcytosine modification (DALRD3), the v-ATPase A subunit (ATP6V1A), a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling RNA-binding protein (CELF2), a trans-Golgi network protein required for peptide hormone processing (HID1), a microtubule-associated serine-threonine kinase (MAST3), an inhibitory component of the mTOR pathway (DEPDC5), the anaphase-promoting complex subunit Cdh1 (FZR1), an ESCRT-II subunit (SNF8), the BRCA1-associated ATM activator (BRAT1), and the neuron-specific beta subunit of the AP-3 vesicle coat adaptor (AP3B2). AP3B2 is placed here rather than at the synaptic node because the AP-3 complex acts in organelle and vesicle biogenesis rather than at the synapse itself. Each functional assignment is taken from the publication cited on that subtype's own has_subtypes row. The node is kept separate from the ion-channel and synaptic lesion node because the two classes reach the shared excitation-inhibition and neurodevelopmental arms by different routes, not because the subtypes here are milder.

evidence.snippet: Many genes mutated in DEEs encode ion channels, causing current conduction disruptions known as channelopathies.
evidence.explanation: Supports the channelopathy arm in which the genetic lesion alters neuronal excitability, the proximate cause of excitation-inhibition imbalance.

steps/58.description: Depending on the specific gene and variant, the molecular lesion produces either a gain- or loss-of-function shift in neuronal excitability (e.g. gain-of-function SCN2A/SCN8A sodium-channel variants causing neuronal hyperexcitability versus loss-of-function SCN1A variants preferentially impairing GABAergic interneuron firing), converging on a common circuit-level disruption of the balance between excitatory and inhibitory synaptic drive.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are the most severe group of epilepsies, characterized by drug-resistant seizures and developmental slowing or regression.
evidence.explanation: The ILAE operational definition identifies drug-resistant seizures as a defining clinical output of the DEE network mechanism.

steps/59.description: Excitation-inhibition imbalance produces hypersynchronous, epileptiform cortical network activity, manifesting clinically as frequent, often multiple, drug-resistant seizure types with an abnormal interictal EEG background.

evidence.snippet: many other mechanisms have been identified: impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders, disruption of dendrite and axon growth, maintenance and synapse formation abnormalities -synaptopathies.
evidence.explanation: Documents the non-channelopathy, neurodevelopmental mechanisms that constitute this seizure-independent arm of the DEE mechanism.

steps/60.description: Independent of seizure activity, the same channel or synaptic-gene defect disrupts activity-dependent synaptic pruning, circuit maturation, and neuronal migration/connectivity during critical developmental windows, producing a developmental encephalopathy component that is not fully reversible by seizure control alone.

evidence.snippet: on a background of developmental impairment that tends to worsen as a consequence of epilepsy
evidence.explanation: States the epileptic-encephalopathy component explicitly: the epilepsy itself worsens developmental impairment.

evidence.snippet: New terminology is introduced such as developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: The 2017 ILAE classification introduced the DEE term precisely to separate the epileptic from the developmental contribution to the encephalopathy.

steps/61.description: Frequent seizures and ongoing epileptiform discharges themselves contribute to cognitive slowing, developmental regression, and behavioral disturbance, over and above the effect of the underlying genetic lesion. This component can partially improve with effective seizure control.

evidence.snippet: What sets DEEs apart is their complex interplay of epilepsy and developmental delay, often driven by genetic factors. These two aspects influence one another but can develop independently, creating diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports modeling the developmental component as a separate arm that can arise independently of the seizure burden - the conceptual basis for splitting these two nodes.

steps/62.description: Developmental delay, intellectual disability, and often autistic features that arise directly from the genetic etiology's disruption of neurodevelopment, and that may be present even before seizure onset or persist despite adequate seizure control.

evidence.snippet: characterised by seizures and frequent epileptiform activity associated with developmental slowing or
evidence.explanation: Developmental slowing or regression is a defining, near-universal feature of the DEE group.

steps/63.description: Developmental slowing or frank regression, which by definition of the DEE concept may precede, coincide with, or follow seizure onset.

evidence.snippet: Patients have wide-ranging comorbidities including intellectual disability, psychiatric
evidence.explanation: Intellectual disability is listed first among the wide-ranging comorbidities of the DEE group.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are the most severe group of epilepsies, characterized by drug-resistant seizures and developmental slowing or regression.
evidence.explanation: Drug resistance is part of the ILAE operational definition of the DEE group.

steps/65.description: Multiple seizure types that are typically refractory to antiseizure medication, a defining feature of the DEE group.

evidence.snippet: The cohort comprised 510 individuals with a genetic DEE, in whom we observed CSE in 47% and NCSE in 19%.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies convulsive and nonconvulsive status epilepticus in a large cohort restricted to genetic DEE, making it directly on-scope for this umbrella entry.

evidence.snippet: The highest proportion of CSE occurred in patients with SCN1A-associated DEEs, including 181/203 (89%; 95% CI 84-93) patients with Dravet syndrome
evidence.explanation: Documents the gene-dependent variation in status epilepticus risk, highest in SCN1A-related disease.

steps/66.description: Convulsive and nonconvulsive status epilepticus are frequent and life-threatening complications, affecting roughly half and one fifth of patients respectively across genetic DEE cohorts, with the highest burden in SCN1A-related disease.

evidence.snippet: characterized by drug-resistant seizures and developmental slowing or regression
evidence.explanation: Developmental regression is named in the ILAE operational definition of the DEE group.

evidence.snippet: It is characterized by early-onset, drug-resistant epilepsy, abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) findings, and developmental delay or regression.
evidence.explanation: Independently corroborates developmental regression as a defining feature of DEE.

steps/67.description: Loss of previously acquired developmental skills, distinct from static delay. Regression is the more severe pole of the developmental encephalopathy component and is part of the operational definition of DEE.

evidence.snippet: characterized by early-onset, often severe epileptic seizures and EEG abnormalities
evidence.explanation: EEG abnormality is named as a core characteristic of the DEE group.

steps/68.description: Frequent epileptiform activity and abnormal interictal EEG background; specific patterns (burst-suppression, hypsarrhythmia) are gene- and age-dependent.

evidence.snippet: features, such as autism spectrum disorder and behavioural problems, movement and musculoskeletal
evidence.explanation: Autism spectrum disorder is named among the psychiatric comorbidities of the DEE group.

evidence.snippet: movement and musculoskeletal disorders, gastrointestinal and sleep problems, together with
evidence.explanation: Movement and musculoskeletal disorders are listed among the wide-ranging DEE comorbidities.

evidence.snippet: Across DEE cohorts, movement disorders occurred in roughly one-quarter to over one-half of patients, were often hyperkinetic (notably dystonia and stereotypies), and frequently combined multiple phenomenologies.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how often movement disorders occur across DEE cohorts and names their predominant hyperkinetic phenomenology, which the comorbidity-list quote above does not.

steps/70.description: Movement and musculoskeletal problems are a recognized comorbidity domain of the DEE group, prominent in specific genetic forms such as GNAO1-related DEE.

evidence.snippet: There were 42/510 (8%) deaths among the cohort, producing a mortality rate of 6.1 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 4.4-8.3). Cases of SUDEP accounted for 19/42 (48%) deaths.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies overall mortality and the SUDEP share in a large genetic DEE cohort.

evidence.snippet: disorders, gastrointestinal and sleep problems, together with  an increased mortality rate.
evidence.explanation: An increased mortality rate is an explicit feature of the DEE group.

steps/71.description: Markedly elevated premature mortality, with sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) the leading identifiable cause in genetic DEE cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Genetic DEEs have been associated with mutations in many genes involved in different functions including cell migration, proliferation, and organization, neuronal excitability, and synapse transmission and plasticity.
evidence.explanation: Connects the causal genes to neuronal excitability and synaptic transmission, the substrate of excitation-inhibition balance.

edges/56.description: The gene-level lesion alters neuronal excitability or synaptic signalling, shifting the excitation-inhibition balance of the network.

evidence.snippet: Many genes mutated in DEEs encode ion channels, causing current conduction disruptions known as channelopathies.
evidence.explanation: Links the channel-level conduction disruption to the epileptic output of the disease.

edges/57.description: Excitation-inhibition imbalance drives the seizure arm of the DEE mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These two aspects influence one another but can develop independently, creating diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.
evidence.explanation: Supports branching the mechanism into two arms that can develop independently of one another.

edges/58.description: The same molecular lesion independently disrupts circuit maturation, producing the developmental arm.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are the most severe group of epilepsies, characterized by drug-resistant seizures and developmental slowing or regression.
evidence.explanation: Names drug-resistant seizures as the defining clinical output of the DEE mechanism, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/59.description: The hypersynchronous network state is what is observed clinically as the antiseizure-medication-refractory seizures that the ILAE operational definition puts at the centre of the DEE concept.

evidence.snippet: The cohort comprised 510 individuals with a genetic DEE, in whom we observed CSE in 47% and NCSE in 19%.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies status epilepticus as an outcome of the seizure mechanism in a cohort restricted to genetic DEE.

edges/60.description: Status epilepticus is the failure of a seizure to self-terminate. Convulsive status epilepticus was recorded in 47 per cent and nonconvulsive status epilepticus in 19 per cent of a 510-patient genetic DEE cohort.

evidence.snippet: characterized by early-onset, often severe epileptic seizures and EEG abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Pairs the seizures and the EEG abnormality as joint characteristics of the DEE group, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/61.description: The same hypersynchrony is recorded interictally as frequent epileptiform activity on an abnormal EEG background, which is the electrographic rather than the clinical reading of this node.

evidence.snippet: on a background of developmental impairment that tends to worsen as a consequence of epilepsy
evidence.explanation: States that the epilepsy itself worsens developmental impairment, the defining claim of this causal edge.

edges/62.description: Ongoing seizures and epileptiform activity themselves degrade cognitive and behavioural function.

evidence.snippet: many other mechanisms have been identified: impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders, disruption of dendrite and axon growth, maintenance and synapse formation abnormalities -synaptopathies.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the neurodevelopmental mechanisms that generate the developmental encephalopathy component.

edges/63.description: Disrupted circuit maturation yields developmental delay and intellectual disability independently of seizure burden.

evidence.snippet: on a background of developmental impairment that tends to worsen as a consequence of epilepsy
evidence.explanation: States that the epilepsy itself worsens developmental impairment, which is the deterioration this edge asserts.

edges/64.description: What this component adds is deterioration: worsening of development on a background of established impairment, rather than the delay itself. That is why loss of previously acquired skills is routed from here rather than from the developmental component, which the entry treats as the source of the delay.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of neuropediatric diseases associated with epileptic seizures, severe delay or regression of psychomotor development, and cognitive and behavioral deficits.
evidence.explanation: Names severe delay of psychomotor development as a defining feature of the DEE group, alongside and separable from the seizures.

edges/65.description: Delayed acquisition of milestones is the direct expression of this component, and in the DEE concept it may precede seizure onset.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of neuropediatric diseases associated with epileptic seizures, severe delay or regression of psychomotor development, and cognitive and behavioral deficits.
evidence.explanation: Names cognitive deficits as a defining feature of the DEE group, alongside and separable from the seizures.

evidence.snippet: Intellectual disability is severe and complicates potential treatment.
evidence.explanation: Characterises the severity of the intellectual disability this edge produces.

edges/66.description: The cognitive endpoint of the developmental arm. Its features may persist despite adequate seizure control, which is the clinical observation that makes this arm separable from the epileptic one.

evidence.snippet: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are a group of neuropediatric diseases associated with epileptic seizures, severe delay or regression of psychomotor development, and cognitive and behavioral deficits.
evidence.explanation: Names behavioural deficits as a feature of the DEE group. It does not separate the developmental from the epileptic contribution, hence INDIRECT.

evidence.snippet: Patients have wide-ranging comorbidities including intellectual disability, psychiatric features, such as autism spectrum disorder and behavioural problems, movement and musculoskeletal disorders, gastrointestinal and sleep problems, together with  an increased mortality rate.
evidence.explanation: Names autism spectrum disorder among the comorbidities of the DEE group. The review states co-occurrence and attributes no mechanism, hence INDIRECT.

edges/67.description: Autistic features are routed from the developmental rather than the epileptic arm because they are part of the cognitive and behavioural phenotype of the underlying genetic lesion. The sources cited here name autism spectrum disorder and behavioural deficits as features of the DEE group without attributing them to either arm, so the routing is this entry's model rather than a claim either source makes.

evidence.snippet: Across DEE cohorts, movement disorders occurred in roughly one-quarter to over one-half of patients, were often hyperkinetic (notably dystonia and stereotypies), and frequently combined multiple phenomenologies.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies movement disorders across DEE cohorts and gives their predominant hyperkinetic character. The review reports co-occurrence rather than a mechanism, hence INDIRECT.

evidence.snippet: Eight cohort studies and multiple tier 2-3 series and reviews yielded 245 single-gene associations, most mapping to ion channel and synaptic signaling pathways.
evidence.explanation: Places the epilepsy-dyskinesia gene set in the same ion-channel and synaptic classes as this entry's upstream lesion nodes, which is the basis for routing the movement disorder from the developmental arm.

edges/68.description: Movement disorders are routed from the developmental arm because most of the epilepsy-dyskinesia genes map to the same ion-channel and synaptic pathways as the upstream lesion nodes, rather than arising from the seizure burden. The cited review reports co-occurrence and gene-pathway membership; it does not test which arm produces the movement disorder, so this edge is an inference from the entry's two-component model.

evidence.snippet: many other mechanisms have been identified: impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders, disruption of dendrite and axon growth, maintenance and synapse formation abnormalities -synaptopathies.
evidence.explanation: States that impaired neurogenesis, metabolic disorders and disrupted dendrite and axon growth are DEE mechanisms, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/69.description: A lesion in metabolic, transport, proteostasis, RNA-processing, cytoskeletal or genome-maintenance machinery disrupts circuit maturation directly, producing the developmental arm without requiring a primary change in channel conduction.

evidence.snippet: Genetic DEEs have been associated with mutations in many genes involved in different functions including cell migration, proliferation, and organization, neuronal excitability, and synapse transmission and plasticity.
evidence.explanation: Places neuronal excitability among the functions disrupted by the wider set of genetic DEE genes, supporting this edge from a non-channel lesion.

edges/70.description: The same non-channel lesions also reach excitation-inhibition balance, either by limiting the supply of neurotransmitter precursors and the ion gradients that neuronal firing depends on, or by altering neuronal excitability directly.

evidence.snippet: Cases of SUDEP accounted for 19/42 (48%) deaths.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the share of deaths attributable to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, which is the seizure-mediated route this edge asserts.

edges/71.description: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy accounted for 19 of 42 deaths in a 510-patient genetic DEE cohort, so ongoing seizures are a proximate route from this phenotype to premature death.

evidence.snippet: genetic cause is found in >50% of patients using next generation sequencing technologies.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that a genetic etiology is identified in the majority of DEE patients, justifying the genetic DEE umbrella as the dominant subgroup.

genes/0.notes: Pathogenic variants causing genetic DEE have been reported in more than nine hundred genes; the most frequent recurring categories are voltage-gated ion channel genes (SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, KCNQ2, KCNA2, KCNT1), presynaptic vesicle-cycle genes (STXBP1, DNM1, SNAP25), and postsynaptic neurotransmitter-receptor genes (GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B), with most cases arising from de novo dominant variants. Individual gene-defined forms are curated as separate dismech entries.

evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.
evidence.explanation: Identifies KCNQ2 among the most frequently identified causal genes in a clinical DEE exome cohort.

genes/1.notes: Kv7.2 voltage-gated potassium channel subunit underlying the neuronal M-current; among the most frequently identified genes in DEE diagnostic cohorts.

evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.
evidence.explanation: Identifies CDKL5 among the most frequently identified causal genes in a clinical DEE exome cohort.

genes/2.notes: X-linked serine/threonine kinase required for activity-dependent synaptic maturation; loss of function causes CDKL5 deficiency disorder, an exemplar of the seizure-independent developmental arm of DEE.

evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.
evidence.explanation: Identifies SCN1A among the most frequently identified causal genes in a clinical DEE exome cohort.

genes/3.notes: Nav1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel, predominantly expressed in GABAergic interneurons; haploinsufficiency causes Dravet syndrome, the archetypal genetic DEE, via interneuron disinhibition. The single most frequently implicated gene in molecularly diagnosed genetic DEE cohorts.

evidence.snippet: The most frequently reported genes in the survey were SCN1A (16%), followed by KCNQ2 (5.6%) and SCN2A (5%).
evidence.explanation: Establishes SCN2A among the three most frequently implicated genetic DEE genes.

genes/4.notes: Nav1.2 voltage-gated sodium channel, predominantly in excitatory neurons. Illustrates the gain- versus loss-of-function dichotomy that drives genotype-guided prescribing: gain-of-function variants cause severe early-infantile DEE responsive to sodium-channel blockers, whereas loss-of-function variants give a later-onset, autism-predominant phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Four genes were associated with SUDEP: SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, and STXBP1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SCN8A as a genetic DEE gene and specifically one carrying SUDEP risk.

genes/5.notes: Nav1.6 voltage-gated sodium channel; DEE-causing variants are typically gain-of-function, and like SCN2A this makes sodium-channel blockers rational rather than contraindicated. One of four genes associated with SUDEP in a large genetic DEE cohort.

evidence.snippet: We included patients with a pathogenic variant in the genes SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, SYNGAP1, NEXMIF, CHD2, PCDH19, STXBP1, GRIN2A, KCNT1, and KCNQ2
evidence.explanation: Lists PCDH19 among the frequently observed genetic DEE genes assembled for a dedicated genetic DEE cohort study.

genes/6.notes: X-linked protocadherin-19. Notable for a female-restricted inheritance pattern in which heterozygous females are affected and hemizygous males are typically unaffected transmitting carriers; the mechanism is curated on the PCDH19 Clustering Epilepsy child entry.

evidence.snippet: KCNQ2, CDKL5, SCN1A, and STXBP1 were the most frequently identified genes.
evidence.explanation: Identifies STXBP1 among the most frequently identified causal genes in a clinical DEE exome cohort.

genes/7.notes: Syntaxin-binding protein 1 (Munc18-1), a core regulator of SNARE-mediated synaptic vesicle fusion; haploinsufficiency impairs both excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter release.

evidence.snippet: DOCK7 codes for a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor that has been implicated in the genesis and polarization of newborn pyramidal neurons and in the morphological differentiation of GABAergic interneurons in the developing cortex.
evidence.explanation: States the neurodevelopmental function through which the DOCK7 lesion reaches the pathograph.

genes/8.notes: HGNC names this gene dedicator of cytokinesis 7. Biallelic truncating variants cause DEE23; the cited report describes DOCK7 as a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor implicated in the genesis and polarization of newborn pyramidal neurons and in the differentiation of cortical GABAergic interneurons.

evidence.snippet: We report two additional cases of ITPA-associated neurodegeneration and two pathogenic compound heterozygous variants.
evidence.explanation: Documents biallelic (compound heterozygous) ITPA variants in further patients.

genes/9.notes: HGNC names this gene inosine triphosphatase. Biallelic variants cause a purine pathway defect presenting as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with a lethal course.

evidence.snippet: Most cases were females carrying the recurrent ALG13 de novo variant, p.(Asn107Ser), with normal transferrin electrophoresis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the recurrent allele, the female predominance, and the normal glycosylation screen.

genes/10.notes: HGNC names this gene ALG13 UDP-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase subunit. The recurrent de novo p.(Asn107Ser) missense variant accounts for most reported ALG13-related DEE, predominantly in females, with normal transferrin electrophoresis.

evidence.snippet: Loss of FRRS1L function attenuates AMPA-mediated currents, implicating chronic abnormalities of glutamatergic neurotransmission in this monogenic neurological disease of childhood.
evidence.explanation: States the glutamatergic mechanism by which the FRRS1L lesion acts.

genes/11.notes: AMPA receptor outer-core protein. Biallelic loss-of-function variants attenuate AMPA-mediated currents and cause an epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with prominent choreoathetosis.

evidence.snippet: Five cases of NTRK2-related DEE were identified. Four had a previously described recurrent variant in NTRK2 and one had a novel variant.
evidence.explanation: Establishes NTRK2 as causal for DEE in a reported case series.

genes/12.notes: HGNC names this gene neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 2, with TRKB as an alias symbol. A recurrent variant accounts for most reported cases of NTRK2-related DEE, which presents with infantile spasms evolving to multifocal seizures, microcephaly and optic nerve hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in A Disintegrin And Metalloproteinase (ADAM) 22, the postsynaptic cell membrane receptor for the glycoprotein leucine-rich repeat glioma-inactivated protein 1 (LGI1), have been recently associated with recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: States both the recessive gene-disease relationship and the postsynaptic LGI1-receptor function that places it in the synaptic arm.

genes/13.notes: Postsynaptic receptor for LGI1. Biallelic inactivating variants cause DEE61 through loss of membrane expression, impaired LGI1 binding, or impaired interaction with PSD-95; the same trans-synaptic complex is affected in the LGI1 subtype DEE121.

evidence.snippet: This study confirms the role of TRAK1 in mitochondrial dynamics and constitutes the first report of this gene in association with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TRAK1 as a neurodevelopmental disease gene acting through mitochondrial dynamics.

genes/14.notes: HGNC names this gene trafficking kinesin protein 1; the cited report describes the TRAK family's role in lysosomal and mitochondrial trafficking. Biallelic truncating variants cause a fatal infantile encephalopathy, and patient fibroblasts show disordered mitochondrial distribution, motility and respiration.

evidence.snippet: Acute knockdown of mouse Phactr1 using in utero electroporation caused defects in cortical neuron migration during corticogenesis, which were rescued by an RNAi-resistant PHACTR1 but not by the four mutants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cortical neuron migration defect through which the PHACTR1 lesion reaches the pathograph, with the mutant alleles failing to rescue.

genes/15.notes: HGNC names this gene phosphatase and actin regulator 1. De novo missense variants cause infantile epileptic spasms syndrome; the variants impair either actin binding or binding to protein phosphatase 1, and mouse knockdown shows defective cortical neuron migration.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate that the RNF13 variants confer gain of function to the encoded protein and thereby lead to altered signaling of the ER stress response associated with severe neurodegeneration in infancy.
evidence.explanation: States the gain-of-function ER-stress mechanism by which the RNF13 lesion acts.

genes/16.notes: HGNC names this gene ring finger protein 13; the cited report describes it as an IRE1-alpha-interacting protein. De novo heterozygous gain-of-function variants increase ER stress signalling and stress-induced apoptosis, causing congenital microcephaly with infantile epileptic encephalopathy and blindness.

evidence.snippet: Our study provides further evidence for validating the role of PARS2 in the pathology of related infantile-onset encephalopathy, contributing to the phenotypic features of this condition, and providing clinical and molecular insight for the diagnosis of this disease entity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PARS2 as causal for infantile-onset encephalopathy, in the report that widened its phenotype.

genes/17.notes: Prolyl-tRNA synthetase 2, a member of the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase family that the cited report describes as critical to protein biosynthesis. Biallelic variants cause an infantile-onset encephalopathy with epileptic spasms, postnatal microcephaly, elevated lactate and progressive cerebral atrophy.

evidence.snippet: Here, we provide additional genetic and clinical data on three new cases that support the pathogenic role of ACTL6B gene mutation in a syndromic form of DEE.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ACTL6B as causal for a syndromic DEE.

genes/18.notes: HGNC names this gene actin like 6B; the cited report describes it as a subunit of the neuron-specific nBAF chromatin remodelling complex. Biallelic variants cause early-onset severe DEE with brain hypomyelination and cerebellar atrophy.

evidence.snippet: The X-linked FHF2 gene (also known as FGF13) has alternative first exons which produce multiple protein isoforms that differ in their N-terminal sequence.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the FGF13/FHF2 identity and X-linkage recorded for this subtype.

genes/19.notes: Fibroblast growth factor homologous factor 2 (FHF2), whose FHF2A isoform the cited report identifies as a regulator of Nav channel function; the gene is X-linked. Missense variants in the N-terminal domain of FHF2A act through gain of function on neuronal excitability.

evidence.snippet: We tested 14 mutations in transfected COS-1 cells and demonstrated impaired NKA-pump activity, consistent with severe loss of function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes loss of Na+/K+-ATPase pump function as the molecular consequence.

genes/20.notes: One of the two Na+/K+-ATPase alpha-subunit isoforms implicated in this spectrum. Heterozygous variants that severely impair pump activity cause a profound epileptic encephalopathy with polymicrogyria or progressive brain atrophy, distinct from the familial hemiplegic migraine and alternating hemiplegia phenotypes curated in other dismech entries.

evidence.snippet: We describe nine new patients with FBXO28 pathogenic variants (four missense, including one recurrent, three nonsense, and one frameshift) and analyze all 10 known cases to delineate the phenotypic spectrum. All patients had epilepsy and 9 of 10 had DEE, including infantile spasms (3) and a progressive myoclonic epilepsy (1).
evidence.explanation: Establishes FBXO28 as a monogenic cause of DEE.

genes/21.notes: HGNC names this gene F-box protein 28. It is one of the two genes in the 1q41-q42 microdeletion interval already implicated in monogenic disease, and heterozygous variants cause DEE with profound intellectual disability and hyperkinetic movement disorders.

evidence.snippet: Our data support the contention that SLC38A3 is a novel disease gene for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and illuminate the likely pathophysiology of the disease as perturbations in glutamine homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SLC38A3 as a DEE gene acting through glutamine homeostasis.

genes/22.notes: SNAT3, a sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter. Biallelic variants perturb glutamine homeostasis; glutamine is the precursor of both GABA and glutamate, which is how this transport lesion reaches excitation-inhibition balance.

evidence.snippet: Five affected subjects with biallelic variants in this gene presented with a phenotype of early-onset progressive myoclonus epilepsy with ataxia, while 12 individuals carried de novo missense variants and showed severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ATP6V0A1 as causal for DEE and records the genotype-phenotype split.

genes/23.notes: Subunit a1 of the V0 domain of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, the brain-enriched isoform. De novo missense variants cause severe DEE, while biallelic variants give progressive myoclonus epilepsy with ataxia; the recurrent R740Q change impairs endolysosomal acidification.

evidence.snippet: Different UFSP2 variants cause markedly different diseases, with homozygosity for V115E causing a severe syndrome of neurodevelopmental disability and epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the recessive UFSP2 neurodevelopmental phenotype as a distinct disease from the dominant skeletal one.

genes/24.notes: UFM1-specific peptidase 2, a de-UFMylating enzyme. Homozygosity for the N-terminal-domain p.V115E variant causes a severe neurodevelopmental disability with epilepsy, distinct from the autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasias caused by catalytic-domain variants.

evidence.snippet: Thus, biallelic loss-of-function variants in CACNA2D1 underlie the severe neurodevelopmental disorder in these two patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic CACNA2D1 loss of function as causal, placing the lesion in the calcium-channel arm.

genes/25.notes: α2δ-1 auxiliary subunit of CaV1 and CaV2 voltage-gated calcium channels. Biallelic loss-of-function variants severely impair its function as a calcium channel subunit and cause early-onset DEE.

evidence.snippet: Levetiracetam, which binds to SV2A, was not effective as an antiepileptic medication.
evidence.explanation: Records that the drug whose target this gene encodes did not control the proband's seizures.

genes/26.notes: Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A and the binding site of levetiracetam. A single homozygous R383Q missense variant in one consanguineous family is the whole reported basis of this subtype; levetiracetam was ineffective in the proband.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report that recurrent germline mutations in RNU2-2 (previously known as pseudogene RNU2-2P), a 191-bp gene that encodes the U2-2 snRNA, are responsible for a related disorder.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene, its former pseudogene designation, and its causal role.

genes/27.notes: U2-2 small nuclear RNA of the major spliceosome. HGNC renamed this locus from RNU2-2P to RNU2-2 on 2024-11-15 (live HGNC REST lookup for HGNC:10152 returns symbol RNU2-2 with RNU2-2P as a previous symbol); the OBO HGNC build this repository validates against still carries RNU2-2P, so term.label is the build's label while preferred_term is the current approved symbol. Recurrent de novo variants at nucleotide positions 4 and 35 cause DEE119; no missplicing was detected in patient blood.

evidence.snippet: Using whole exome/genome sequencing, we identified de novo missense variants in BAIAP2 in six patients with DEEs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes BAIAP2 as a causal DEE gene.

genes/28.notes: Brain-specific angiogenesis inhibitor 1-associated protein 2, acting in dendritic spine morphogenesis and excitatory synapse formation. De novo missense variants clustered in the multiple phosphorylation site region act by gain of function, increasing excitatory synaptogenesis and neuronal excitability.

evidence.snippet: LGI1 is a secreted neuronal protein, functions as a ligand for ADAM22/23, and regulates excitatory synaptic transmission and neuronal excitability in the brain.
evidence.explanation: States the synaptic mechanism through which the LGI1 lesion reaches neuronal excitability.

genes/29.notes: Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated protein 1, a secreted ligand for ADAM22 and ADAM23. Biallelic variants that reduce secretion and ADAM22 binding cause DEE121; monoallelic variants cause autosomal dominant epilepsy with auditory features, curated in the Autosomal_Dominant_Epilepsy_with_Auditory_Features entry.

evidence.snippet: we mapped the disease locus to chromosome 19q13.33 and identified multiple mutations in PNKP (polynucleotide kinase 3'-phosphatase) that result in severe neurological disease; in contrast, a splicing mutation is associated with more moderate symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PNKP as the causal gene and records the allele-dependent severity.

genes/30.notes: Polynucleotide kinase 3'-phosphatase. Biallelic variants cause MCSZ; a splicing allele is associated with a milder course. The allelic PNKP peripheral-nerve phenotype is curated in Charcot-Marie-Tooth_Disease_Type_2B2.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a cohort of 4 patients with epileptic encephalopathy and heterozygous de novo missense variants in SCN3A (p.Ile875Thr in 2 cases, p.Pro1333Leu, and p.Val1769Ala).
evidence.explanation: Establishes SCN3A as causal for DEE62.

genes/31.notes: HGNC names this gene sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 3. The cited report identifies Nav1.3 as highly expressed in brain and previously unlinked to early infantile epileptic encephalopathy; de novo missense variants produce gain of channel function.

evidence.snippet: We identified novel KCNC2 variants in 18 patients with various forms of epilepsy, including genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) including early-onset absence epilepsy, focal epilepsy, and myoclonic-atonic epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes KCNC2 as causal across a spectrum whose severe pole is DEE103.

genes/32.notes: HGNC names this gene potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily C member 2. The cited report describes Kv3.2 as a Shaw-related voltage-gated potassium channel subunit important for sustained high-frequency firing; the DEE pole of the KCNC2 spectrum is associated with gain of function.

evidence.snippet: We report a cohort of 17 patients, including 9 with a recurrent de novo missense variant p.Arg327His, 4 with a recurrent missense variant p.Arg333His, and 4 additional novel missense variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the KCNH5 variant series behind DEE112.

genes/33.notes: HGNC names this gene potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily H member 5. The cited report describes KCNH5 as encoding the voltage-gated potassium channel EAG2/Kv10.2; the DEE phenotype is associated with specific recurrent variants rather than with the gene as a whole.

evidence.snippet: We report on 2 females with de novo variants in KCNT2 with West syndrome followed by Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or with DEE with migrating focal seizures.
evidence.explanation: Establishes KCNT2 as causal for DEE57.

genes/34.notes: HGNC names this gene potassium sodium-activated channel subfamily T member 2. The paralogue of KCNT1. De novo variants act by gain of function and were quinidine-responsive in vitro and in one treated patient.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe 17 unrelated individuals with severe early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), intellectual disability, and severe motor and cortical visual impairment associated with progressive neurodegenerative brain changes carrying ten distinct heterozygous variants of TMEM63B, encoding for a highly conserved stretch-activated ion channel.
evidence.explanation: Establishes TMEM63B as causal for this DEE and names the channel class.

genes/35.notes: HGNC names this gene transmembrane protein 63B. The cited report describes TMEM63B as a highly conserved stretch-activated ion channel; the mutated channels carry an inward leak cation current under isotonic conditions.

evidence.snippet: By combining these strategies, we were able to provide a causal link between DEE and the following genes: NTRK2, GABRB2, CLTC, DHDDS, NUS1, RAB11A, GABBR2, and SNAP25.
evidence.explanation: Establishes GABRB2 as causal for DEE.

genes/36.notes: HGNC names this gene gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor subunit beta2. One of eight genes given a causal link to DEE by the cited whole-genome study of unexplained DEE trios. That study characterises no GABRB2-specific phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Targeted resequencing of 279 additional epilepsy patients identified 19 rare variants from nine GABAA receptor genes, including a novel de novo missense variant in GABRA2 (c.875C > A, p.T292K) and a recurrent missense variant in GABRB3 (c.902C > T, p.P301L).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the de novo GABRA2 variant causal for DEE78.

genes/37.notes: HGNC names this gene gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor subunit alpha2. The cited report describes GABA-A receptors as ligand-gated anion channels regulating neuronal inhibition; the p.Thr292Lys variant reduced channel expression and left the channel tonically open in the absence of GABA.

evidence.snippet: Using whole-genome sequencing, we identified a novel de novo missense variant in GABRA5 (c.880G > C, p.V294L) in a patient with severe early-onset epilepsy and developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the de novo GABRA5 variant causal for DEE79.

evidence.snippet: By combining these strategies, we were able to provide a causal link between DEE and the following genes: NTRK2, GABRB2, CLTC, DHDDS, NUS1, RAB11A, GABBR2, and SNAP25.

The metabotropic GABA-B receptor subunit, so a lesion of GABAergic inhibition rather than of a voltage-gated channel. First seen in two DEE trios as suggestive evidence; the causal link came from a later whole-genome study.

evidence.snippet: Using exome sequencing, we identified four individuals with a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy and de novo missense variants in SLC32A1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes de novo SLC32A1 variants as causal for DEE114.

evidence.snippet: Herein, we, for the first time, document human monogenic disease phenotype of de novo pathogenic variants in NSF, that is, epileptic encephalopathy of early infantile onset.

The cited report describes NSF as critical for intracellular vesicle transport underlying neurotransmitter release, and reads the de novo variants as dominant negative on the strength of a Drosophila eye assay.

evidence.snippet: Variant prioritization identified a homozygous nonsense variant in the N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein, beta (NAPB) gene resulting in a premature stop codon and 46% loss of the protein.

evidence.snippet: We performed whole exome or genome sequencing in three independent sib pairs with early onset refractory seizures and progressive neurological decline, and identified novel segregating recessive SYNJ1 defects.

evidence.snippet: We report bi-allelic pathogenic mutations in MDH2 in three unrelated subjects presenting with early-onset generalized hypotonia, psychomotor delay, refractory epilepsy, and elevated lactate in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid.

genes/44.notes: HGNC names this gene malate dehydrogenase 2. Mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase, which converts malate to oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Patient fibroblasts lost MDH2 protein with enzymatic activity close to null and accumulated malate and fumarate.

evidence.snippet: We have now identified biallelic CNPY3 variants in three individuals with WS; these include compound-heterozygous missense and frameshift variants in a family with two affected siblings (individuals 1 and 2) and a homozygous splicing variant in a consanguineous family (individual 3).

genes/45.notes: HGNC names this gene canopy FGF signaling regulator 3. An endoplasmic reticulum co-chaperone that regulates the subcellular distribution and responses of multiple Toll-like receptors. Protein was severely reduced in lymphoblastoid cells from two affected siblings.

evidence.snippet: We identify a recurrent de novo CUX2 p.Glu590Lys as a novel genetic cause for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE).

genes/46.notes: HGNC names this gene cut like homeobox 2. A cut homeodomain transcription factor with a role in dendrite branching, spine development and synapse formation in layer II to III cortical neurons. The recurrent p.Glu590Lys variant lies in the CUT domain and is predicted to interfere with DNA binding.

evidence.snippet: Ten cases with heterozygous de novo mutations in the SMC1A gene are presented. All 10 mutations identified are predicted to result in premature truncation of the SMC1A protein.
evidence.explanation: Establishes truncating SMC1A variants as causal for DEE85.

genes/47.notes: HGNC names this gene structural maintenance of chromosomes 1A. A core structural subunit of the cohesin complex, so this is a cohesinopathy. evidence.snippet: Notably, we identify a homozygous nonsense mutation in the DALRD3 gene that impairs m3C formation in human patients exhibiting developmental delay and early-onset epileptic encephalopathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the homozygous DALRD3 lesion as causal for DEE86 and names the tRNA-modification defect.

genes/48.notes: HGNC names this gene DALR anticodon binding domain containing 3. Forms a complex with the METTL2 methyltransferase that selects particular arginine tRNA isoacceptors for 3-methylcytosine modification of the anticodon loop.

evidence.snippet: Through whole exome sequencing, we identified de novo heterozygous mutations (p.Pro27Arg, p.Asp100Tyr, p.Asp349Asn, p.Asp371Gly) in ATP6V1A, encoding the A subunit of v-ATPase, in four patients with developmental encephalopathy with epilepsy.

genes/49.notes: HGNC names this gene ATPase H+ transporting V1 subunit A. The A subunit of the vacuolar proton ATPase, which sets organellar pH and has additional roles at the neuronal synapse. Severity in the founding four patients tracked the individual variant.

evidence.snippet: We report heterozygous CELF2 (NM_006561.3) variants in five unrelated individuals: Individuals 1-4 exhibited developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) and Individual 5 had intellectual disability and autistic features.
evidence.explanation: Establishes heterozygous CELF2 variants as causal for DEE97.

genes/50.notes: HGNC names this gene CUGBP Elav-like family member 2. A nucleocytoplasmic shuttling RNA-binding protein with roles in RNA processing and in development of the central nervous system and heart. The pathogenic variants cluster at the C-terminal nuclear localisation signal and mislocalise the protein out of the nucleus.

evidence.snippet: Bi-allelic variants in the gene HID1 domain-containing protein 1 (HID1) were identified in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic HID1 variants as causal for DEE105.

genes/51.notes: HGNC names this gene HID1 domain containing. Acts in the trans-Golgi network where peptide hormone precursors are processed, which is why the biallelic lesion pairs an epileptic encephalopathy with central pituitary insufficiency.

evidence.snippet: We identify de novo missense variants in the STK domain in 11 individuals, including 2 recurrent variants p.G510S (n = 5) and p.G515S (n = 3).
evidence.explanation: Establishes de novo MAST3 kinase-domain variants as causal for DEE108.

genes/52.notes: HGNC names this gene microtubule associated serine/threonine kinase 3. One of the microtubule-associated serine-threonine kinases, expressed in excitatory cortical neurons late in prenatal development and postnatally. Transfected cells showed increased phosphorylation of the MAST3 target ARPP-16, read as gain of function.

evidence.snippet: We describe a novel phenotype caused by germline biallelic missense variants in DEPDC5.
evidence.explanation: Establishes germline biallelic DEPDC5 variants as causal for DEE111 and separates them from the heterozygous focal-epilepsy phenotype.

genes/53.notes: HGNC names this gene DEP domain containing 5, GATOR1 subcomplex subunit. An inhibitory component of the mTOR pathway. The common germline lesion is a single inactivating heterozygous variant, curated as the separate DEPDC5-Related_Epilepsy entry; the biallelic germline lesion curated here gives bilateral polymicrogyria with macrocephaly instead of a focal lesion.

evidence.snippet: In this study, evaluation of 250 unrelated patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathies and a connection on GeneMatcher led to the identification of three de novo missense variants in FZR1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes de novo FZR1 variants as causal for DEE109.

genes/54.notes: HGNC names this gene fizzy and cell division cycle 20 related 1. Encodes Cdh1, a substrate-recognition subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex, with roles in the cell cycle and in post-mitotic neurons. Drosophila assays supported the patient variants being loss of function.

evidence.snippet: We report nine individuals from six families presenting with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental/neurodegenerative features caused by bi-allelic variants in SNF8 (GenBank: NM_007241.4), encoding the ESCRT-II subunit SNF8.
