genes/55.notes: HGNC names this gene SNF8 subunit of ESCRT-II. A subunit of ESCRT-II, one of the three endosomal sorting complexes required for membrane remodelling and autophagy. The milder pole of the SNF8 spectrum is curated as SNF8-Related_Neurodevelopmental_Disorder.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype correlations in our cohort revealed that biallelic nonsense, frameshift or inframe deletion/insertion variants result in the severe BRAT1-related RMFSL phenotype (46/46; 100%). genes/56.notes: HGNC names this gene BRCA1 associated ATM activator 1. Biallelic variants give two distinct phenotypes, and the genotype largely predicts which: nonsense, frameshift or in-frame indel genotypes give the lethal rigidity and multifocal-seizure phenotype, while genotypes including a missense variant usually give the non-lethal cerebellar-atrophy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: AP3B2 encodes the neuron-specific subunit of the AP-3 complex.

genes/57.notes: HGNC names this gene adaptor related protein complex 3 subunit beta 2. The neuron-specific beta subunit of the AP-3 vesicle coat adaptor complex. The ubiquitous isoform AP3B1 causes Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 instead, which is why the AP3B2 phenotype is purely neurological.

evidence.snippet: Holistic management, which encompasses antiseizure therapies and care for multimorbidities, is determined both by epilepsy syndrome and aetiology.

evidence.snippet: Understanding the functional consequences of the SCN1A pathogenic variant informs management, as some sodium channel blocker (SCB) antiseizure medications (ASMs) may exacerbate seizures in Dravet syndrome, whereas patients with the non-Dravet, EIDEE phenotype due to GOF variants may respond to SCB, such as carbamazepine and phenytoin

evidence.snippet: The ketogenic diet (KD) is a well-established non-pharmacological treatment for refractory epilepsy and has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in several DEE subtypes.

evidence.snippet: In certain cases, it may reduce or even eliminate the need for pharmacological interventions.

evidence.snippet: The ketogenic diet (KD) is a well-established non-pharmacological treatment for refractory epilepsy and has demonstrated therapeutic efficacy in several DEE subtypes.

evidence.snippet: The higher dose of fenfluramine was associated with a significantly greater likelihood of achieving a >50% (68% versus 12% placebo) and a >75% reduction (50% versus 2% placebo) in convulsive seizure frequency
evidence.explanation: RCT evidence of dose-dependent convulsive-seizure reduction, targeting the seizure node.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Symptomatic suppression of seizure generation via serotonergic modulation.

evidence.snippet: In Dravet syndrome, a RCT of stiripentol demonstrated clear efficacy

CHEBI has no stiripentol term, so the agent is bound to NCIT following the documented NCIT-fallback convention for drugs lacking a CHEBI entry.

evidence.snippet: In Dravet syndrome, a RCT of stiripentol demonstrated clear efficacy

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Symptomatic suppression of seizure generation, used in combination with clobazam.

evidence.snippet: Identification of the underlying aetiology enables the development of precision medicines to improve the long-term outcome of patients with these devastating diseases.
evidence.explanation: Supports molecular diagnosis as the enabler of precision therapy in the DEE group.

evidence.snippet: Finding the molecular cause led to management changes in 36% of patients with DEEs.

evidence.snippet: Identification of the underlying aetiology enables the development of precision medicines to improve the long-term outcome of patients with these devastating diseases.
evidence.explanation: Supports the aetiology-directed link from molecular diagnosis back to the causal genetic lesion node.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: The only entry-level treatment addressing the upstream cause rather than the seizure output. Establishing the specific gene and the functional direction of the variant redirects therapy at the lesion itself, and is the gateway to gene-targeted modalities (antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapy) still in development.

evidence.snippet: Adult-type diffuse gliomas represent a group of highly infiltrative central
evidence.explanation: Adult-type diffuse gliomas are highly infiltrative CNS tumors of glial lineage.

steps/0.description: Gliomas arise from neoplastic transformation of glial cells or glial/neural stem and progenitor cells, producing highly infiltrative (diffuse) or circumscribed CNS tumors. Cell-of-origin lineage (astrocytic, oligodendroglial, ependymal, or mixed neuronal-glial) together with molecular alterations underpins the WHO CNS5 integrated diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: For the first time molecular features are not only relevant for the classification of IDH-mutant gliomas but may impact grading as well.
evidence.explanation: IDH mutation is the defining molecular feature separating IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype gliomas and informs grading.

evidence.snippet: D-2-HG promotes DNA and histone hypermethylation.
evidence.explanation: The IDH-mutant oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate drives DNA and histone hypermethylation, the epigenetic reprogramming underlying the glioma CpG-island methylator phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Diagnosis of adult type diffuse gliomas, IDH
evidence.explanation: WHO CNS5 anchors adult-type diffuse glioma diagnosis on IDH mutation status.

steps/1.description: IDH1 or IDH2 mutation is the primary biological divider of adult-type diffuse glioma. Mutant IDH acquires neomorphic activity producing the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which competitively inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases (TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases), yielding a glioma CpG-island methylator phenotype and a block in glial differentiation. IDH-mutant tumors carry a more favorable prognosis than IDH-wildtype.

evidence.snippet: bind the mutated TERT promoter and upregulate TERT expression
evidence.explanation: RNA polymerase II binding the mutated TERT promoter upregulates TERT expression, reactivating telomerase and enabling telomere maintenance in glioma.

steps/2.description: TERT promoter mutation reactivates telomerase, enabling telomere maintenance and replicative immortality. TERT promoter mutation is one of the three glioblastoma-defining molecular markers (with EGFR amplification and +7/-10) and also occurs frequently in oligodendroglioma.

evidence.snippet: EGFR amplification, and TERT promoter mutation are diagnostic
evidence.explanation: EGFR amplification is one of the glioblastoma-defining molecular alterations under WHO CNS5 (diagnostic of grade 4 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma). The RTK-RAS-PI3K signaling mechanism this node also describes still needs a dedicated source.

steps/3.description: EGFR amplification (often with the EGFRvIII variant) and related receptor tyrosine kinase lesions drive constitutive RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR mitogenic signaling and growth-factor-independent proliferation. EGFR amplification is one of the three glioblastoma-defining molecular features.

evidence.snippet: whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion and TERT promoter
evidence.explanation: Whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion is a defining large-scale chromosomal copy-number alteration under WHO CNS5, exemplifying the copy-number changes this node describes.

steps/4.description: Glioma types are defined in part by large-scale chromosomal copy-number alterations: combined whole chromosome 7 gain and chromosome 10 loss (+7/-10) and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma; whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion in oligodendroglioma; and CDKN2A/B loss upgrading IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4. These reflect underlying chromosomal instability.

evidence.snippet: Adult-type diffuse gliomas represent a group of highly infiltrative central
evidence.explanation: Diffuse gliomas are characterized by highly infiltrative growth in the CNS.

steps/5.description: Diffuse gliomas grow by single-cell infiltration of brain parenchyma along white-matter tracts and perivascular/subpial routes, precluding complete surgical resection and driving recurrence despite therapy.

edges/0.description: Transformed glial-lineage cells acquire the canonical molecular lesions that define glioma type.

edges/1.description: Transformed cells acquire TERT promoter mutation, a glioblastoma-defining lesion enabling replicative immortality.

edges/2.description: Transformed cells acquire large-scale copy-number alterations (+7/-10, 1p/19q codeletion, CDKN2A/B loss) that define glioma type and grade.

edges/3.description: Transformed cells acquire EGFR amplification (a glioblastoma-defining lesion) driving constitutive mitogenic signaling.

edges/4.description: Transformed cells infiltrate brain parenchyma along white-matter tracts.

edges/6.description: Sustained mitogenic signaling promotes tumor cell proliferation and invasion.

edges/7.description: Chromosomal instability drives clonal evolution that sustains tumor progression and infiltrative growth.

genes/1.notes: IDH2 mutation is a less common alternative to IDH1 mutation and produces the same D-2-hydroxyglutarate oncometabolite; it likewise defines IDH-mutant adult-type diffuse glioma.

genes/3.notes: EGFR amplification (frequently with EGFRvIII) is one of three glioblastoma-defining molecular features and activates RTK-RAS-PI3K signaling.

genes/4.notes: Whole-arm codeletion of chromosomes 1p and 19q, together with IDH mutation, defines oligodendroglioma. This is a chromosomal codeletion, not a single-gene lesion, so it carries no gene_term.

genes/5.notes: Homozygous deletion of CDKN2A (with the adjacent CDKN2B) is a WHO CNS5 grade-4 criterion in IDH-mutant astrocytoma and is common in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.

genes/6.notes: CDKN2B is co-deleted with CDKN2A at 9p21; homozygous CDKN2A/B loss upgrades IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4 and is frequent in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.

evidence.explanation: About 10% of adult-type diffuse glioma patients harbored pathogenic germline variants in a paired tumor/normal series.

genes/7.notes: Most gliomas are sporadic, but a clinically meaningful minority carry pathogenic germline variants (e.g., BRCA2, MUTYH, CHEK2, NF1, mismatch-repair genes), with implications for surveillance and cascade testing.

evidence.explanation: Chemotherapy (temozolomide) with radiotherapy is standard of care for high-grade glioma.

evidence.explanation: Adding TTFields to standard chemoradiotherapy significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.63).

evidence.snippet: Fluoxetine treatment has a clear antiaggressive effect in impulsive aggressive individuals with IED.
evidence.explanation: A randomized placebo-controlled response to serotonin reuptake inhibition supports serotonergic involvement only through an inference step from treatment response back to mechanism, so this is recorded as indirect.

steps/0.description: Reduced central serotonergic tone is the longest-standing neurochemical model of impulsive aggression in IED. Direct human synaptic evidence is limited; the strongest clinical support is pharmacologic, in that selective serotonin reuptake inhibition reduces impulsive aggression in IED without acting through an antidepressant or anxiolytic effect.

evidence.snippet: Gray matter volume was found to be significantly lower in subjects with IED compared with healthy control subjects and psychiatric controls in orbitofrontal cortex, ventral medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, insula, and uncus.
evidence.explanation: Volumetric MRI study establishes the frontolimbic structural deficit in IED against both healthy and psychiatric comparison groups.

evidence.snippet: Gray matter volume in these areas was significantly and inversely correlated with measures of aggression.
evidence.explanation: Relationship between regional volume and aggression severity strengthens the link between this structural finding and the aggressive phenotype.

steps/1.description: Voxel-based morphometry in 57 subjects with IED, compared with both healthy and psychiatric control groups, shows lower gray matter volume across the orbitofrontal cortex, ventral medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, insula and uncus, with volume inversely correlated with aggression measures.

evidence.snippet: Relative to controls, individuals with IED exhibited exaggerated amygdala reactivity and diminished OFC activation to faces expressing anger.
evidence.explanation: Task-based fMRI directly measures the exaggerated amygdala response to an ecologically valid social threat signal in IED.

steps/2.description: Functional MRI during viewing of emotionally salient faces shows exaggerated amygdala responses to angry faces in unmedicated subjects with IED relative to matched healthy comparison subjects.

evidence.snippet: Relative to controls, individuals with IED exhibited exaggerated amygdala reactivity and diminished OFC activation to faces expressing anger.
evidence.explanation: The same contrast reports the reduced orbitofrontal response that this node describes.

steps/3.description: The same social-emotional probe shows diminished orbitofrontal cortex activation to angry faces in IED, the regulatory counterpart of the amygdala finding.

evidence.snippet: Unlike controls, aggressive subjects failed to demonstrate amygdala-OFC coupling during responses to angry faces.
evidence.explanation: Directly reports the connectivity failure that distinguishes this node from the two regional activation abnormalities upstream of it.

steps/4.description: Beyond the two regional abnormalities individually, aggressive subjects fail to show the normal functional coupling between amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex during processing of angry faces, indicating a breakdown of top-down regulation rather than two independent deficits.

evidence.snippet: In addition, IED participants displayed reduced encoding of relevant information from the film clips, elevated hostile attribution bias, elevated negative emotional response, and elevated endorsement of physically aggressive and relationally aggressive responses to the ambiguous social-emotional stimuli presented in the V-SEIP.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that IED participants show elevated hostile attribution bias on a validated social-emotional information processing assessment.

steps/5.description: Individuals with IED over-attribute hostile intent to ambiguous social-emotional stimuli and generate more aggressive response options, a social-emotional information processing bias that sits between the frontolimbic circuit abnormality and the aggressive behavioral output. It is the cognitive bias the cognitive-behavioral intervention targets.

steps/6.description: The convergent clinical consequence of the frontolimbic deficit is a failure to resist aggressive impulses when provoked, producing outbursts disproportionate to the provocation. Outbursts are impulsive and anger-based rather than premeditated.

evidence.snippet: Intermittent explosive disorder-related injuries occurred 180 times per 100 lifetime cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the injurious consequences of the recurrent aggressive outbursts in a nationally representative sample.

steps/7.description: The defining manifestation of IED: repeated failures to control aggressive impulses, with a mean of 43 lifetime attacks and frequent resulting injury and property damage.

evidence.snippet: Secondary efficacy measures included the irritability score from the OAS-M and the Clinical Global Impressions-Improvement scale (CGI-I) score.
evidence.explanation: Trial design treats OAS-M irritability as a measured clinical dimension of IED.

steps/8.description: Irritability is assessed as a core clinical dimension of IED alongside overt aggression, and improves with serotonergic treatment.

evidence.snippet: Intermittent explosive disorder (IED) is a disorder of impulsive aggression that affects as many as 7.3% of the U.S. population during some period of life.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes IED aggression as impulsive, the feature this phenotype records.

steps/9.description: Aggression in IED is impulsive rather than premeditated, which is what separates it from instrumental or planned aggression.

evidence.snippet: Primary study outcomes were aggressive behavior and anger.
evidence.explanation: Randomized trial treats anger as a primary clinical outcome dimension in IED.

steps/10.description: Outbursts are anger-based, and anger is a primary outcome dimension in IED treatment trials.

edges/0.description: Reduced serotonergic modulation is proposed to leave amygdala-driven threat responses inadequately restrained; the intervening steps are not established in humans.

edges/1.description: Reduced prefrontal gray matter is proposed as the anatomic correlate of the functional regulatory deficit; the studies are cross-sectional and do not establish the direction of causation.

evidence.snippet: These findings provide evidence of amygdala-OFC dysfunction in response to an ecologically-valid social threat signal (processing angry faces) in individuals with a history of impulsive aggressive behavior, and further substantiate a link between a dysfunctional cortico-limbic network and aggression.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion asserts the link between the cortico-limbic dysfunction described by this node and aggressive behavior, which is the edge rather than either node alone.

evidence.snippet: In addition, IED participants displayed reduced encoding of relevant information from the film clips, elevated hostile attribution bias, elevated negative emotional response, and elevated endorsement of physically aggressive and relationally aggressive responses to the ambiguous social-emotional stimuli presented in the V-SEIP.
evidence.explanation: Links the elevated hostile attribution bias in IED to elevated endorsement of aggressive responses, the mechanistic step from this node to the behavioral output.

evidence.snippet: Fluoxetine treatment resulted in a sustained reduction in OAS-M aggression, and OAS-M irritability scores, apparent as early as week 2 (p < .01 for aggression and p < .001 for irritability at endpoint).
evidence.explanation: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 100 subjects with IED reports the primary and secondary efficacy results.

evidence.snippet: However, while fluoxetine's antiaggressive effects appear robust, they lead to full or partial remission of IED in less than 50% of subjects treated with fluoxetine.
evidence.explanation: The same trial bounds the magnitude of benefit, which is why this treatment is described as partial rather than curative.

treatments/0.description: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibition reduces impulsive aggression and irritability in IED. The effect is robust but partial: fewer than half of treated subjects reach full or partial remission, and the antiaggressive effect is independent of any antidepressant or anxiolytic action.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Fluoxetine acts by enhancing serotonergic transmission, the mechanism this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Though participants in both treatments tended to improve over time, the cognitive behavioral intervention was superior to supportive psychotherapy in decreasing aggressive behavior and relational aggression.
evidence.explanation: Randomized controlled trial against an active comparator supports specific efficacy of the cognitive behavioral intervention.

treatments/1.description: A twelve-session multicomponent cognitive behavioral intervention targeting anger, cognitive bias and relational aggression was superior to a time-equated supportive psychotherapy control in adults with IED.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: The intervention targets the behavioral endpoint of the frontolimbic chain rather than an upstream neurochemical step.

evidence.snippet: In yeast, the MECR-R258W mutant showed an impaired oxidative growth, 30% reduction in oxygen consumption rate and 80% decrease in protein levels, pointing to structure destabilisation.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that a recurrent missense allele destabilizes the MECR protein, reducing its activity.

steps/3.description: Biallelic pathogenic MECR variants (missense, nonsense, or splice-site) reduce or abolish mitochondrial trans-2-enoyl-CoA/ACP reductase activity, the enzyme that carries out the terminal NADPH-dependent reduction step of mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis. Missense alleles typically act as destabilizing hypomorphs rather than complete nulls.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) is an evolutionarily conserved pathway essential for the function of the respiratory chain and several mitochondrial enzyme complexes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes mtFAS as the pathway disabled in MEPAN and its role supporting the respiratory chain and enzyme complexes.

steps/4.description: Loss of MECR activity impairs the terminal step of mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS), reducing production of acyl-ACP species including octanoyl-ACP, the precursor of lipoic acid, and of longer-chain acyl-ACPs required for mitochondrial complex assembly.

evidence.snippet: Among the fatty acids synthesised by mtFAS, there is octanoic acid, the precursor of lipoic acid (LA), a cofactor involved in the activity of several mitochondrial enzymes, among which the pyruvate dehydrogenase, the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, the branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase, the 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage system.
evidence.explanation: States that mtFAS-derived octanoic acid is the lipoic acid precursor, linking mtFAS failure to lipoic acid deficiency.

steps/5.description: Octanoic acid (octanoyl-ACP) produced by mtFAS is the precursor of lipoic acid, an essential cofactor for several mitochondrial 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes; reduced octanoyl-ACP lowers lipoic acid availability.

evidence.snippet: Fibroblast cell lines from affected individuals displayed reduced levels of both MECR and lipoylated proteins as well as defective respiration.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived fibroblasts directly demonstrate reduced protein lipoylation downstream of MECR deficiency.

steps/6.description: Reduced lipoic acid availability causes failure to lipoylate the lipoate-dependent mitochondrial enzymes; patient fibroblasts and mouse brain both show reduced levels of lipoylated proteins.

evidence.snippet: Among the fatty acids synthesised by mtFAS, there is octanoic acid, the precursor of lipoic acid (LA), a cofactor involved in the activity of several mitochondrial enzymes, among which the pyruvate dehydrogenase, the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, the branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase, the 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage system.
evidence.explanation: Names the lipoate-dependent enzymes (PDH, KGDH, BCKDH, glycine cleavage) whose function depends on the lipoic acid supplied by mtFAS.

steps/7.description: Deficient lipoylation impairs the lipoate-dependent 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes - pyruvate dehydrogenase and 2-oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate) dehydrogenase among them - compromising oxidative decarboxylation flux into the TCA cycle.

evidence.snippet: LC-MS/MS-based proteomic analysis of Mecr mutant cerebella identified loss of subunits of complex I of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and subunits of the iron-sulfur cluster assembly (ISC) complex.
evidence.explanation: The MEPAN mouse shows loss of ISC assembly and complex I subunits, supporting the ISC/supercomplex branch.

steps/8.description: Loss of properly acylated acyl-carrier protein (ACP) destabilizes the mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) assembly complex and alters oxidative-phosphorylation complex and supercomplex assembly, an ACP-acylation-dependent branch demonstrated in Mecr-mutant mouse brain and in fly models.

evidence.snippet: We observe a defect in Fe-S cluster biogenesis and increased iron levels in flies lacking mecr, leading to elevated ceramide levels. Reducing the levels of either iron or ceramide suppresses the neurodegenerative phenotypes, indicating an interplay between ceramide and iron metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Interventional fly evidence that iron and ceramide dysregulation drives the neurodegeneration.

evidence.snippet: we show that human-derived fibroblasts display similar elevated ceramide levels and impaired iron homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived fibroblasts corroborate the elevated-ceramide/iron mechanism in human cells.

steps/9.description: Downstream of the Fe-S cluster biogenesis defect, mecr-loss neurons accumulate free iron and elevated ceramide; lowering either iron or ceramide suppresses the neurodegenerative phenotype, and MEPAN patient fibroblasts replicate the elevated-ceramide/impaired-iron signature. This branch is established primarily in a Drosophila model with patient-fibroblast corroboration.

evidence.snippet: The MEPAN mouse recapitulates the major hallmarks of MEPAN, including a movement disorder, optic neuropathy, defects in protein lipoylation, and reduced mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in the brain.
evidence.explanation: The mouse model demonstrates reduced brain oxidative phosphorylation as the bioenergetic lesion.

steps/10.description: The combined loss of lipoate-dependent flux, ISC-dependent respiratory enzymes, and OXPHOS supercomplex integrity produces a mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation deficit, measured as defective respiration in patient fibroblasts and reduced OXPHOS in Mecr-mutant mouse brain.

evidence.snippet: Seven individuals from five unrelated families presented with childhood-onset dystonia, optic atrophy, and basal ganglia signal abnormalities on MRI.
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort ties basal-ganglia involvement to the dystonic movement disorder.

steps/11.description: Selective neurodegeneration of the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus), reflected clinically as dystonia and chorea and radiologically as T2-hyperintense basal-ganglia signal, is the substrate of the extrapyramidal movement disorder.

evidence.snippet: Fundus exam revealed bilateral optic atrophy with pallor most pronounced temporally, corresponding to OCT findings of diffuse retinal nerve fiber layer thinning most prominent in the papillomacular bundle region and severe ganglion cell layer thinning in the maculae.
evidence.explanation: Ophthalmic imaging demonstrates retinal ganglion cell layer loss underlying the optic atrophy.

steps/12.description: Degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons in the papillomacular bundle produces the optic atrophy, with a pattern resembling other mitochondrial optic neuropathies (LHON, dominant optic atrophy).

evidence.snippet: The mitochondria in KO PCs displayed abnormal morphology, loss of protein lipoylation, and reduced respiratory chain enzymatic activities by the time these mice were 6 months of age, followed by nearly complete loss of PCs by 9 months of age.
evidence.explanation: A Purkinje-cell-specific Mecr knockout shows Purkinje-cell degeneration, the model basis for cerebellar involvement.

steps/13.description: MECR is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells, and Purkinje-cell degeneration - established in a Purkinje-cell-specific Mecr knockout mouse - is a plausible substrate for the ataxia that accompanies the movement disorder in a subset of patients. The Purkinje-cell mechanism is model-derived; the ataxia phenotype itself is documented clinically.

evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent homozygous p.Arg258Trp allele underlying phenotypic heterogeneity.

treatments/2.description: Multidisciplinary supportive care - visual aids for reduced acuity, occupational and physical therapy to maintain mobility, speech therapy and augmentative communication for dysarthria, and feeding support - plus annual ophthalmologic, neurologic, speech, cognitive and feeding surveillance. Stress and febrile illness should be minimized as they are presumed to exacerbate progression.

evidence.snippet: With lipoic acid treatment, the disease progression was under control, and neither visual impairment nor optic atrophy was observed.
evidence.explanation: Anecdotal single-patient report of stabilized progression on lipoic acid.

evidence.snippet: feeding the mice with medium chain triacylglycerols and LA affected fatty acid profiles in the cerebellum and plasma but did not prevent the development of neurodegeneration in these mice.
evidence.explanation: A controlled mouse study found medium-chain triglyceride plus lipoic acid supplementation did not prevent neurodegeneration, tempering the anecdotal human benefit.

treatments/3.description: Because the mtFAS defect lowers lipoic acid synthesis, lipoic acid (with or without octanoic acid / medium-chain triglyceride supplementation) has been tried as a mechanism-targeted therapy. Evidence is limited and mixed: a single homozygous p.Asp304Tyr patient had controlled progression without developing optic atrophy on lipoic acid, but medium-chain triglyceride plus lipoic acid feeding did not prevent neurodegeneration in a Purkinje-cell Mecr-knockout mouse. It is investigational and should not be presented as established disease-modifying therapy.

evidence.snippet: With lipoic acid treatment, the disease progression was under control, and neither visual impairment nor optic atrophy was observed.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Exogenous lipoic acid is intended to counter the deficient endogenous lipoic acid synthesis by supplying the cofactor directly. The strategy is mechanism-targeted but investigational, with only anecdotal human benefit and a negative controlled mouse result.

evidence.snippet: In human patients, most of the currently known pathogenic NDUFS4 mutations lead to absence of (full length) NDUFS4 protein
evidence.explanation: The allelic mechanism, stated across the reported human mutation spectrum rather than for one variant.

evidence.snippet: In the mutation that was expected to produce a truncated subunit, the disappearance of the protein was associated with an almost complete disappearance of the NDUFS4 transcript.
evidence.explanation: Why a predicted truncating allele behaves as a null: the transcript goes too. Graded IN_VITRO because the measurement is in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: An identity-by-descent mapping and candidate gene approach was used to identify a novel homozygous c.393dupA frameshift mutation in the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) Fe-S protein 4 (NDUFS4) gene.
evidence.explanation: A founder frameshift allele in a defined population.

evidence.snippet: The carrier frequency of this mutation was estimated in >1,300 Hutterite individuals to be 1 in 27.
evidence.explanation: The carrier frequency, which is a population-specific figure and not a general NDUFS4 carrier rate.

evidence.snippet: One parent lacked the variant, and microsatellite genotyping showed complete paternal uniparental isodisomy of the non-imprinted chromosome 5.
evidence.explanation: A route to biallelic NDUFS4 loss that carrier testing of both parents would miss.

steps/1.description:
The reported pathogenic alleles are frameshifts, nonsense variants and splice-altering variants, and what they have in common is more informative than what distinguishes them: almost all of them abolish full-length NDUFS4 protein. Where a truncated product would be predicted, the transcript itself is usually lost as well.
Founder alleles exist. A homozygous c.393dupA frameshift accounts for Leigh disease in the Hutterite population, where the carrier frequency was estimated at 1 in 27 across more than 1,300 individuals, and founder alleles have also been described in North Africa. A non-consanguineous family reached homozygosity by complete paternal uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 5, which is worth knowing because a single-parent carrier test in that situation is falsely reassuring.

evidence.snippet: the current experimental data suggests that the NDUFS4 subunit is potentially PKA-phosphorylated and plays a key role in CI assembly and/or stabilization (likely involving N-to-Q-module attachment), thereby exerting control over CI levels and/or activity.
evidence.explanation: The function of the subunit, stated as the review's synthesis across structural and biochemical studies rather than as a single experiment - which is why this item is graded OTHER.

evidence.snippet: Within ovine CI, the NDUFS4 subunit is located at the interface between the N- and Q-module
evidence.explanation: The structural position that the assembly role follows from, determined in the ovine enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Absence of NDUFS4 induced near complete absence of the NDUFA12 accessory subunit, a 50% reduction in other CI subunit levels, and an increase in specific CI assembly factors.
evidence.explanation: The knock-on loss of NDUFA12 and the accumulation of assembly factors, measured across Ndufs4-null mouse tissues - which is why this item is MODEL_ORGANISM while the next one, quoting the sentence about patient cells, is IN_VITRO.

evidence.snippet: Regarding NDUFS4, NDUFA12 and NDUFAF2, identical results were obtained in Ndufs4-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and NDUFS4-mutated LS patient cells.
evidence.explanation: The step that makes the mouse biochemistry transferable: the same subunit losses were measured in human patient cells.

steps/2.description:
NDUFS4 is one of about thirty accessory subunits of complex I, and its position is what makes it load-bearing. It sits at the interface between the N module, which oxidises NADH, and the Q module, which passes the electrons to ubiquinone, and it contacts subunits in both. The current reading of the experimental data is that NDUFS4 controls the attachment of the N module to the rest of the enzyme.
Losing it takes a second subunit with it. In both Ndufs4-null mouse cells and NDUFS4-mutant patient cells the accessory subunit NDUFA12 is almost entirely absent, while the assembly factor NDUFAF2 - which NDUFA12 would normally displace - accumulates. The relationship is one-way: NDUFA12-mutant patient cells do not lose NDUFS4.

evidence.snippet: NDUFS4-mutated patient fibroblasts exhibit complete absence of the fully assembled CI holocomplex.
evidence.explanation: The native-gel result in human patient cells.

evidence.snippet: All NDUFS4 mutations that have been tested with BN-PAGE result in a constant and similar abnormal assembly profile with a complete loss of the fully assembled complex I usually due to a truncated protein and the loss of its canonical cAMP dependent protein kinase phosphorylation consensus site.
evidence.explanation: The constancy across alleles, from a systematic study plus a literature meta-analysis.

evidence.snippet: Ndufs4-/- MEFs contained active CI in situ but blue-native-PAGE highlighted that NDUFAF2 attached to an inactive CI subcomplex (CI-830) and inactive assemblies of higher MW.
evidence.explanation: The caveat in the node description: active enzyme in situ alongside no holoenzyme on the gel, which is why the arrest is described as destabilisation rather than total absence.

evidence.snippet: Two-dimensional electrophoresis showed the absence of detectable normally assembled complex I in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence.explanation: The original demonstration, in the first NDUFS4 nonsense patient.

steps/3.description:
On a blue native gel, NDUFS4-mutant patient fibroblasts show no fully assembled complex I holoenzyme at all. What is present instead is a catalytically inactive subcomplex of about 830 kDa, carrying NDUFAF2 and lacking the N module. This profile is constant across every NDUFS4 allele that has been tested, which is unusual enough that it was proposed as a screening method: the gel plus the MRI identifies the gene.
One caveat belongs with the finding. In intact tissue, substantial rotenone-sensitive quinone-reductase activity survives, and Ndufs4-null mouse fibroblasts contain active complex I in situ - so the complete absence of holoenzyme on the gel partly reflects the complex falling apart during solubilisation. The enzyme in a living cell is destabilised, not necessarily wholly absent.

evidence.snippet: In general, the expression/activity of OXPHOS complexes other than CI is not affected by NDUFS4 mutations and/or absence of the NDUFS4 protein.
evidence.explanation: The isolation of the defect to complex I, which is the entity-defining biochemical feature.

evidence.snippet: Fibroblast cultures from the patient exhibited severe reduction of the rotenone-sensitive NADH-->UQ oxidoreductase activity of complex I, which was insensitive to cAMP stimulation.
evidence.explanation: Both halves: the activity loss, and its loss of cAMP responsiveness.

steps/4.description:
The enzymatic consequence, and it is isolated in the strict sense: the expression and activity of the other oxidative phosphorylation complexes are not affected. That is what puts this disease in the complex I deficiency nomenclature rather than in the combined respiratory-chain disorders, and it is measurable in the tissues that are biopsied - muscle in 18 of 22 reported patients, fibroblasts in 12.
In a patient fibroblast line, complex I activity is severely reduced and, distinctively, insensitive to cAMP stimulation - the NDUFS4 subunit carries the consensus site through which protein kinase A is thought to act on the complex.

evidence.snippet: increased reactive oxygen species and NAD(P)H levels, aberrations in cytosolic and mitochondrial calcium/ATP homeostasis and altered mitochondrial morphology
evidence.explanation: The cell-biological consequences measured in NDUFS4-mutant patient cells. The membrane depolarisation that opens the same sentence in the source is omitted from the quotation only because it is written with a non-ASCII symbol; it is stated in the node description.

evidence.snippet: Comprehensive metabolomic profiling revealed a distinct metabolic phenotype in NDUFS4 KO iPSCs, predominantly associated with an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio, consistent with alterations observed in other models of mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: The reductive-stress readout in a human isogenic knockout.

evidence.snippet: Western blotting confirmed the absence of NDUFS4 protein in KO iPSCs and CI enzyme kinetics showed a ~56 % reduction in activity compared to isogenic controls.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the activity loss against a defined isogenic control.

steps/5.description:
Downstream of the enzyme defect, patient-derived cells show partial mitochondrial membrane depolarisation, raised reactive oxygen species and raised NAD(P)H, disturbed cytosolic and mitochondrial calcium and ATP handling, and altered mitochondrial morphology. Pyruvate that cannot be oxidised is converted to lactate, which is what raises lactate in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid.
A CRISPR knockout of NDUFS4 in human induced pluripotent stem cells reproduces the redox half of this directly, with roughly half the complex I activity of isogenic controls and an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio - useful because it is a human cell with a defined isogenic comparator rather than a patient line with an uncontrolled background.

evidence.snippet: Depleting leukocytes with a colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor inhibitor disrupted disease progression, including suppression of CNS lesion formation and a substantial extension of survival.
evidence.explanation: The intervention result the causal claim rests on.

evidence.snippet: these findings dramatically alter our understanding of the pathogenesis of LS, demonstrating that immune involvement is causal in disease.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the claim's strength and scope.

steps/6.description:
Proliferating leukocytes are not just present in the lesions; in the Ndufs4 knockout mouse they are causally required for them. Depleting leukocytes with a CSF1R inhibitor suppressed lesion formation, rescued seizures, respiratory centre function and hyperlactaemia, and substantially extended survival. The same work proposes this as the explanation for why mTOR inhibition works, which had been unexplained for nearly a decade.
Whether this is true of human NDUFS4 disease is untested. It is recorded because a causal immune step changes what a therapy would target, and because it is the strongest single mechanistic result to come out of this model since the rapamycin finding.

evidence.snippet: (iii) lesions of the brainstem (n = 14) and basal ganglia (n = 9); (iv) cortical atrophy (n = 3);
evidence.explanation: The lesion distribution and its counts in the 22-patient NDUFS4 compilation.

evidence.snippet: We also report the association of abnormal brain MRI images with this characteristic BN-PAGE profile as the hallmarks of NDUFS4 mutations
evidence.explanation: The pairing of imaging with the assembly profile as a gene-specific signature.

steps/7.description: The neuropathological endpoint, and the reason most NDUFS4 patients are diagnosed as Leigh syndrome. Brainstem lesions were present in 14 of 22 reported NDUFS4 patients and basal ganglia lesions in 9; cortical atrophy was much less common, in 3. The lesion pattern together with the native-gel profile was proposed as the diagnostic signature of NDUFS4 mutations before sequencing.

evidence.snippet: models suggests that the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in NDUFS4-mutated patients (see above) might be a secondary consequence of the CI deficiency, which develops at a later age.
evidence.explanation: The claim that the cardiac phenotype is secondary and late, drawn from tissue-specific mouse models.

evidence.snippet: Human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPS-CMs) with Ndufs4 deletion recapitulate LS cardiomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: A human cell model of the cardiac phenotype specific to this gene.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate a direct link between complex I deficiency, decreased intracellular (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) NAD+ /NADH and bradyarrhythmia, mediated by hyperacetylation of the cardiac sodium channel NaV 1.5, particularly at K1479 site.
evidence.explanation: The molecular route from the enzyme defect to a cardiac electrical phenotype.

steps/8.description:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy occurs in a minority of NDUFS4 patients - 5 of 22 in the published compilation. Heart- and muscle-specific Ndufs4 knockout mice suggest it is a late, secondary consequence of the complex I defect rather than a primary cardiac lesion, which matters for surveillance: it is something to look for over time rather than at presentation.
An iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte model with NDUFS4 deletion reproduces the cardiac phenotype and links it to a specific molecular step - a fall in NAD+/NADH that leaves the cardiac sodium channel NaV1.5 hyperacetylated, producing bradyarrhythmia.

edges/1.description: The alleles do not produce a variant protein to study; they produce no protein.

edges/2.description: Without NDUFS4 the N module is not docked and the assembly intermediate persists.

edges/5.description: The laboratory finding that establishes the diagnosis biochemically.

edges/6.description: How a cell-autonomous bioenergetic defect recruits or activates leukocytes has not been established; the immune involvement is demonstrated, the step connecting it to the enzyme defect is not.

edges/7.description: The classical account: neurons with the highest energy demand fail first, which is why the lesions are where they are.

edges/8.description: Unoxidised pyruvate is converted to lactate and exported.

edges/9.description: Tissue-specific mouse work places the cardiac phenotype downstream of the complex I defect rather than as an independent lesion.

edges/10.description: Removing the leukocytes removes the lesions, which is a causal rather than an associative claim.

edges/11.description: Loss of acquired milestones follows destruction of the affected grey-matter structures.

edges/12.description: Brainstem respiratory centres are among the structures the lesions involve, which is why breathing failure is the usual terminal event.

edges/13.description: The presenting sign in every reported patient.

edges/14.description: Corticospinal tract involvement within the brainstem lesions, in the minority of patients who show it.

edges/15.description: Reduced visual engagement follows the encephalopathy rather than a specific ocular lesion; the intermediates are the developmental regression and the ocular abnormalities curated alongside it.

edges/16.description: The clinical finding, in the minority of patients who develop it.

evidence.snippet: We describe five new NDUFS4 patients with a similar and constant abnormal BN-PAGE profile and present a meta-analysis of the literature.
evidence.explanation: Five further patients plus a systematic review, which is the evidence that the constancy claim rests on.

evidence.snippet: These findings show that the expression of the NDUFS4 gene is essential for the assembly of a functional complex I.
evidence.explanation: The gene-function conclusion from the founding patient study.

genes/0.notes: The reported alleles are frameshift, nonsense and splice-altering, and nearly all abolish full-length protein - which is why, unusually for a mitochondrial gene, the biochemical consequence is the same whichever allele a patient carries. That homogeneity is the entity's most useful diagnostic property.

evidence.snippet: The current mainstay of managing mitochondrial disease involves the use of vitamin co-factors
evidence.explanation: What is actually given. The snippet is truncated before a non-ASCII character in the source list of cofactors.

evidence.snippet: None of these approaches have demonstrated efficacy in randomized controlled clinical trials.
evidence.explanation: The evidence status of the supplements used, stated plainly by the source.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management is nutritional support for the feeding difficulties present in about a third of patients, seizure control, respiratory monitoring given the frequency of central apnoea, cardiac surveillance for the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that develops in a minority, and rehabilitation. Mitochondrial vitamin and cofactor cocktails are widely used and have not demonstrated efficacy in randomised trials in this or any related condition.

evidence.snippet: We found that rapamycin, a specific inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway, robustly enhances survival and attenuates disease progression in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The survival result. Model evidence only, which is why the description says preclinical.

evidence.snippet: Ndufs4−/− mice show a progressive neurodegenerative phenotype characterized by lethargy, ataxia, weight loss, and ultimately death at a median age of 50 days
evidence.explanation: The untreated baseline the treated survival is measured against.

evidence.snippet: Median survival of males and females was 114 and 111 days, respectively
evidence.explanation: The treated survival on the daily-dosing schedule, so the size of the effect is quoted rather than described.

treatments/1.description:
The landmark preclinical result in this disease and still the most-replicated one. Untreated Ndufs4 knockout mice die at a median of 50 days; on daily rapamycin, median survival was 114 days in males and 111 in females, and the longest-lived animal reached 269. Treatment also delayed the onset of neurological signs, reduced neuroinflammation and prevented the brain lesions altogether in treated animals examined at 100 and 268 days.
It has not been tested in a controlled trial in NDUFS4 patients. The mechanism was unexplained for years and the leukocyte work now offers one - that rapamycin's benefit is largely immunosuppressive.

evidence.snippet: delays onset of neurological symptoms, reduces neuroinflammation, and prevents brain lesions.
evidence.explanation: The effect on neuroinflammation and lesions specifically, in the Ndufs4 model.

evidence.snippet: These data reveal a mechanistic explanation for the beneficial effects of mTOR inhibition.
evidence.explanation: The proposed mechanism linking this treatment to the leukocyte node rather than to the enzyme defect.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: On the emerging account, mTOR inhibition acts by suppressing the leukocyte proliferation that drives lesion formation, rather than by correcting the bioenergetic defect.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, temporary or milder hypoxia conditions (17% O2 for 3 weeks) were ineffective.
evidence.explanation: The negative result that defines how narrow the effective window is, and the practical obstacle to translation.

evidence.snippet: Further preclinical studies are required to assess whether hypoxic exposure can be developed into a safe and effective treatment for human diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of how far this result reaches.

treatments/2.description: Breathing 11% oxygen continuously improves survival, body weight, temperature, behaviour and neuropathology in Ndufs4 knockout mice, and applied late can reverse established brain lesions. The dose-response is unusually strict and is the reason this has not become a clinical intervention: 17% oxygen for three weeks was ineffective, and intermittent hypoxia does not work either. A therapy that requires continuous severe hypoxia is difficult to deliver safely to an infant with brainstem respiratory failure.

evidence.snippet: Chronic hypoxia leads to a marked improvement in survival, body weight, body temperature, behavior, neuropathology, and disease biomarkers in a genetic mouse model of Leigh syndrome
evidence.explanation: The efficacy result in the Ndufs4 model.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Reducing tissue oxygen prevents and can reverse the lesions, without correcting the complex I defect that causes them.

evidence.snippet: NR also attenuated neuronal apoptosis and microglial activation in the LS brain and human iPS-derived neurons with Ndufs4 deletion.
evidence.explanation: The effect in a human cell system, which is the closest this treatment gets to human evidence. Graded IN_VITRO for the iPSC-derived neuron arm.

treatments/3.description: Aimed at the reductive stress rather than at the enzyme. Nicotinamide riboside raised intracellular NAD+/NADH, reversed protein hyperacetylation, improved the cardiomyopathic phenotype and reduced neuronal apoptosis and microglial activation in Ndufs4-null mice, and the same effects were seen in human iPSC-derived neurons with NDUFS4 deletion. Preclinical; no trial in NDUFS4 patients.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic rescue by nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation increased intracellular NAD+ / NADH, restored metabolic derangement, reversed protein hyperacetylation through NAD+ -dependent Sirtuin deacetylase, and ameliorated cardiomyopathic phenotypes
evidence.explanation: The mechanism and the phenotypic effect together.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Raising the NAD+/NADH ratio addresses the redox consequence of the block, leaving the assembly defect in place.

evidence.snippet: However, this vector was absent in the brain and did not ameliorate clinical symptoms.
evidence.explanation: A deliberate negative result, and the reason this treatment is described as a delivery problem rather than a mechanism problem. It refutes the general claim that supplying NDUFS4 is sufficient: an intravenous vector that reaches muscle, heart and liver but not brain does nothing for the disease.

treatments/4.description:
The only strategy here aimed at the lesion itself rather than at its consequences, and the one whose preclinical record most clearly identifies what would stop it working in a patient: getting the vector into the brain.
Several vectors have been tried in Ndufs4-null mice. AAV-PHP.B carrying human NDUFS4, delivered at postnatal day 26 to 28, extended lifespan and reduced disease severity across growth, motor coordination, failure to thrive, seizures and cardiac abnormalities. An AAV1 construct delivered bilaterally into the vestibular nuclei extended lifespan and delayed progression - which is also the observation that implicates those nuclei in the mouse's breathing failure.
The negative result is the informative one. Intravenous AAV2/9 carrying human NDUFS4 reached skeletal muscle, heart and liver, was absent from brain, and did not improve clinical symptoms. A disease whose lesions are in the brainstem is not treated by a vector that stops at the blood-brain barrier, and mouse and human barriers differ, so a delivery route that works in this animal does not transfer by default.

evidence.snippet: Various adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors were used to deliver human NDUFS4 (hNDUFS4)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the strategy as gene replacement of the missing subunit rather than modulation of a downstream process.

evidence.snippet: extended lifespan and reduced disease severity (normalization of growth rate, improvement of motor coordination, preventing development of failure to thrive, epileptic seizures and cardiac abnormalities)
evidence.explanation: The efficacy result for the vector that did reach brain, listing the specific features rescued.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Supplying NDUFS4 protein to cells that make none addresses the molecular lesion directly, upstream of the assembly arrest and everything below it. Whether enough of the brain can be transduced to matter is the unsolved half.

treatments/5.description:
The most recent preclinical strategy and the one that follows from the emerging leukocyte-driven account of lesion formation. In Ndufs4 knockout mice a CSF1R inhibitor suppressed lesion formation, rescued seizures, respiratory function and hyperlactaemia and substantially extended survival.
It has not been tried in patients, and the step it targets has not been demonstrated in human NDUFS4 tissue - so this is a treatment aimed at a mechanism that is itself recorded here as emerging.

evidence.snippet: We show that directly targeting leukocyte proliferation via colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibition dramatically attenuates disease.
evidence.explanation: The intervention and its effect in the model.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Depleting the proliferating leukocyte population removes the step the lesions are argued to require.

hypotheses/0.description: The classical account treats the symmetric necrotizing brainstem lesions as the direct result of energy failure in metabolically demanding neurons. Work in the Ndufs4 knockout mouse argues that immune cells are not merely reacting to that injury but are causally required for it: depleting leukocytes with a CSF1R inhibitor suppressed lesion formation and substantially extended survival, and this also supplies the missing mechanism for why mTOR inhibition helps. It is recorded as emerging because it rests on one model system and has no human validation.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The biochemical match is as good as this field gets. The human alleles abolish the protein, the disease is recessive, and the whole-body knockout reproduces the assembly lesion, including the loss of NDUFA12 and the retained NDUFAF2, measured the same way in mouse and patient cells. That part transfers.
The neuropathology does not transfer as cleanly. The mouse lesions centre on the vestibular nuclei, olfactory bulb and cerebellum. The human disease is defined by brainstem and basal ganglia involvement, with basal ganglia lesions in 9 of 22 reported patients and cortical atrophy in only 3. Seizures are prominent in the terminal phase of some knockout lines but occur in 4 of 22 published patients. The tempo differs too: the mouse is well for five weeks and dies two weeks later, while the median human patient presents at four months and dies at ten.
This matters because every current therapeutic lead in this disease - rapamycin, chronic hypoxia, NAD repletion, leukocyte depletion - was established by preventing lesions in this animal, and the endpoint used was the mouse's own lesion set. If the anatomical distribution reflects a species difference in which nuclei are most vulnerable, an intervention that protects the mouse vestibular nucleus need not protect the human putamen.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The severity claim in this entry comes from a 2016 review that compared 22 NDUFS4 patients against 198 patients with other complex I defects and concluded the NDUFS4 phenotype is invariably early-onset, severe and rapidly fatal. That is the strongest gene-specific prognostic statement available and it is what makes NDUFS4 recognisable within the complex I class.
Since then at least two patients have been reported who do not fit: a girl alive at seven, with a milder course attributed to an intronic splice variant reached through uniparental isodisomy, and an eight-year-old whose presentation was bilateral horizontal gaze palsy. In the 22-patient compilation itself, only 14 had mortality data.
The mechanism that would explain a mild patient is available and untested. The severe phenotype is associated with alleles that abolish the protein entirely; a leaky splice variant that permits some residual NDUFS4 should sit further along the same axis. Nobody has measured residual NDUFS4 protein or complex I assembly in the long-surviving patients, so the correlation between residual protein and survival is a hypothesis rather than a finding.
The stake is counselling. A family told the disease is invariably fatal in infancy is being given a prognosis derived from a series that may systematically miss the children who live.

evidence.snippet: Studies in yeast have shown that a deficiency in Atp12p prevents assembly of the extrinsic domain (F(1)) of complex V and renders cells unable to make ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: The conserved assembly-factor function that the disease allele removes.

evidence.snippet: ATPAF2, the homolog of the yeast Atp12 chaperone that interacts with the α subunit of F1 during assembly of this ATP synthase module
evidence.explanation: The molecular identity of the lost function.

steps/1.description: ATPAF2/Atp12 binds the F1 alpha subunit and prevents nonproductive alpha/beta aggregation during formation of the catalytic alpha3-beta3 hexamer. The W94R substitution destroys this chaperone function — in the humanized yeast system the wild-type human protein rescues an atp12 deletion while the mutant protein is insoluble — so the F1 catalytic head cannot be built.

evidence.snippet: Blue Native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis followed by catalytic staining had already documented their complex V decreased activity.
evidence.explanation: The patient-tissue demonstration of decreased complex V activity.

evidence.snippet: was found to have a homozygous W94R amino acid substitution that resulted in severe deficits of ATP synthase in the heart, liver and to a lesser degree in skeletal muscle, resulting in death at 14 months of age
evidence.explanation: The tissue distribution of the enzyme deficit in the index patient.

steps/2.description: Assembled, catalytically active complex V falls severely in patient tissues — most in liver and heart, less in skeletal muscle — while the other OXPHOS complexes are comparatively preserved, the biochemical signature of an isolated complex V assembly defect.

evidence.snippet: A homozygous c.280T>A substitution in ATPAF2 gene was found in a girl with dysmorphic features, cortical- subcortical brain atrophy followed by basal ganglia atrophy and metabolic acidosis, who died at the age of 14 months.
evidence.explanation: The progressive neurodegenerative and metabolic course of the single case.

steps/3.description: Failure of aerobic ATP synthesis produces lactic acidosis with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, and in the developing brain a progressive degeneration — cortical-subcortical atrophy followed within months by basal ganglia atrophy — with severe developmental impairment. The child died at 14 months during an intercurrent infection, consistent with the heightened vulnerability of mitochondrial disease to catabolic stress.

evidence.snippet: This patient, diagnosed with lactic acidosis, glutaconic aciduria, encephalomyopathy and a range of different developmental problems
evidence.explanation: The encephalomyopathy of the index case as restated by the review.

evidence.snippet: cortical- subcortical brain atrophy followed by basal ganglia atrophy
evidence.explanation: The progressive imaging course of the index case.

steps/4.description: Severe neonatal-onset encephalopathy with marked cortical-subcortical atrophy on MRI, followed within months by basal ganglia and thalamic atrophy. Observed in the single reported patient.

evidence.snippet: This patient, diagnosed with lactic acidosis, glutaconic aciduria, encephalomyopathy and a range of different developmental problems
evidence.explanation: Lactic acidosis in the index case.

evidence.snippet: In this case biosynthesis of ATPase is down-regulated due to a block at the early stage of enzyme assembly-formation of the F(1) catalytic part.
evidence.explanation: The review's statement of the causal step: the assembly block is what produces the enzyme deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Extensive molecular analysis of five nuclear and two mitochondrial genes revealed a mutation in the ATP12 assembly gene in one patient.
evidence.explanation: The index molecular diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: To our knowledge, this is the first report of a pathogenic mutation in a human nuclear encoded ATPase assembly gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the historic priority of ATPAF2 among nuclear assembly-gene causes.

genes/0.notes: ATPAF2 (17p11.2; historically ATP12) encodes a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial matrix protein that chaperones the F1 alpha subunit during assembly of the catalytic alpha3-beta3 hexamer of complex V. One pathogenic allele is known: c.280T>A (p.Trp94Arg), homozygous in the single reported patient. Tryptophan 94 is the most conserved position of the protein.

treatments/0.description: No ATPAF2-specific therapy, trial, or treatment-response report exists. Management is supportive and phenotype-directed, following general mitochondrial-disease practice: nutritional support, antiseizure therapy where needed, and avoidance of fasting and catabolic stress during intercurrent illness.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the results of these studies support a protective effect of vitamin D, but there are uncertainties and many unanswered questions, including how vitamin D exerts a protective effect, how genetic variations modify the effect, and whether vitamin D can influence the course of MS progression.
evidence.explanation: The abstract suggests that adequate vitamin D nutrition can contribute to the prevention of multiple sclerosis, implying that vitamin D deficiency increases the risk.

evidence.snippet: Risk factors for multiple sclerosis: decreased vitamin D level and remote Epstein-Barr virus infection in the pre-clinical phase of multiple sclerosis.
evidence.explanation: The title directly states that decreased vitamin D levels are a risk factor for multiple sclerosis.

evidence.snippet: By analyzing 8,711 individuals, we showed that heterozygote carriers of this low-frequency variant have an increased risk of vitamin D insufficiency... Individuals carrying one copy of this variant also had increased odds of multiple sclerosis...
evidence.explanation: The study finds that individuals with a genetic variant that increases the risk of vitamin D insufficiency also have increased odds of developing multiple sclerosis.

evidence.snippet: New Evidence for Epstein-Barr Virus Infection as a Cause of Multiple Sclerosis.
evidence.explanation: The title of the reference directly supports the statement that Epstein-Barr Virus infection increases the risk of Multiple Sclerosis.

evidence.snippet: The strongest known risk factor for MS is infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Compared with uninfected individuals, the hazard of developing MS is approximately 15-fold higher among individuals infected with EBV in childhood and about 30-fold higher among those infected with EBV in adolescence or later in life.
evidence.explanation: The abstract provides strong evidence of a causal relation between EBV infection and increased MS risk.

evidence.snippet: With recent findings connecting the Epstein-Barr virus to an increased risk of multiple sclerosis... We also replicated the Epstein-Barr/multiple sclerosis association.
evidence.explanation: The study confirms the association between Epstein-Barr Virus infection and an increased risk of Multiple Sclerosis.

evidence.snippet: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a known risk factor for MS and seems to be a prerequisite for disease development.
evidence.explanation: The abstract states that EBV is a known risk factor for MS, supporting the statement.

evidence.snippet: There is strong evidence however that people with MS are more likely to report a past history of infectious mononucleosis (thought to represent initial EBV infection at an older age), and higher titres of EBV specific antibodies are associated with an increased risk of developing MS.
evidence.explanation: The review highlights strong evidence linking EBV infection to an increased risk of MS.

evidence.snippet: MS does not develop in the absence of EBV exposure, and EBV is necessary, but insufficient on its own, to cause disease.
evidence.explanation: The deep-research artifact surfaced this model-organism thesis as an EBV prevention/mechanism result; the snippet supports EBV exposure as a necessary but not sufficient cofactor rather than a sole cause.

evidence.snippet: Risk of MS increased 32-fold after infection with EBV but was not increased after infection with other viruses, including the similarly transmitted cytomegalovirus.
evidence.explanation: The primary longitudinal cohort behind the risk estimate the reviews above report second-hand: more than 10 million US military personnel, 955 of whom developed MS while serving. The comparison with cytomegalovirus, transmitted the same way, is what makes the association specific to EBV rather than to being infection-prone.

evidence.snippet: Here we demonstrate high-affinity molecular mimicry between the EBV transcription factor EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) and the central nervous system protein glial cell adhesion molecule (GlialCAM)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the mimicry itself. Cross-reactivity was identified by single-cell sequencing of the paired-chain B-cell repertoire of MS blood and CSF and then characterized by protein microarray, affinity measurement, and a crystal structure of the EBNA1 epitope bound to the autoreactive Fab - biochemical and structural assays outside an organism, hence IN_VITRO.

evidence.snippet: Blocking experiments confirmed the presence of cross-reactive antibodies and molecular mimicry between EBNA1 and GlialCAM, and accompanying antibody responses against adjacent peptide regions of GlialCAM suggest epitope spreading.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation in 650 MS patients versus 661 matched population controls. Note the authors write that spreading to adjacent GlialCAM regions is suggested, not demonstrated; the OpenScientist report that surfaced this paper overstated that verb.

evidence.snippet: Antibody responses against EBNA1, GlialCAM, CRYAB, and ANO2 are elevated in MS patients carrying the main risk allele HLA-DRB1*15:01
evidence.explanation: Ties the mimicry response to the entry's principal genetic risk factor: the cross-reactive antibody responses are elevated in HLA-DRB1*15:01 carriers, and the combination raises MS risk additively.

steps/10.description: Antibodies raised against the Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) cross-react with the CNS protein glial cell adhesion molecule (GlialCAM), supplying a molecular route from EBV infection of B cells to a CNS-directed adaptive response. The cross-reactivity was found in clonally expanded cerebrospinal-fluid B cells of people with MS and is structurally resolved at the EBNA1 AA386-405 epitope; anti-EBNA1 and anti-GlialCAM responses are elevated in MS and interact with the HLA-DRB1*15:01 risk allele. Whether this mimicry is sufficient to initiate disease, or one of several routes (bystander activation, immortalization of autoreactive B cells) is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) where immunopathology is thought to be mediated by myelin-reactive CD4+ T helper (TH) cells. The TH cells most commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of the disease are of TH1 and TH17 lineage, which are defined by the production of interferon-γ and interleukin-17, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Directly establishes TH1 and TH17 cells as the key drivers of MS immunopathology.

evidence.snippet: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by recurrent episodes of demyelination and axonal lesion mediated by CD4(+) T cells with a proinflammatory Th1 and Th17 phenotype, macrophages, and soluble inflammatory mediators.
evidence.explanation: Confirms Th1 and Th17 phenotypes as mediators of MS demyelination and axonal damage.

evidence.snippet: Autoreactive Th17 cells can migrate through the BBB by the production of cytokines such as IL-17 and IL-22, which disrupt tight junction proteins in the central nervous system (CNS) endothelial cells.
evidence.explanation: Describes the mechanism by which Th17 cells cross the BBB via IL-17 and IL-22 disruption of tight junctions.

steps/11.description: MS immunopathology is mediated by myelin-reactive CD4+ T cells of Th1 and Th17 lineage. Th17 cells produce IL-17, IL-22, and other proinflammatory cytokines that disrupt blood-brain barrier tight junction proteins and recruit neutrophils into the CNS. The IL-23/IL-17 axis amplifies neuroinflammation.

evidence.snippet: Leukocyte entry into the CNS is nonetheless an early event in multiple sclerosis (MS), an inflammatory disorder of the CNS... Immune cells of MS subjects express inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species (ROS) and enzymes that can facilitate their migration to the CNS by influencing BBB function, either directly or indirectly.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the statement that immune cells cross the blood-brain barrier and create inflammation in the central nervous system.

evidence.snippet: During this early stage of the disease, leukocytes cross the blood-brain barrier to drive the formation of focal demyelinating plaques.
evidence.explanation: This reference directly supports the statement by mentioning that leukocytes cross the blood-brain barrier and drive the formation of focal demyelinating plaques, which are inflammatory lesions.

evidence.snippet: Neuroinflammation is triggered when peripheral leukocytes migrate to the central nervous system and release cytokines such as interleukins 1 and 6 (IL-1 and 6) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), which act on dwelling cells.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the statement by explaining that peripheral leukocytes migrate to the CNS and trigger neuroinflammation.

evidence.snippet: Astrocytes are now recognized to be early and highly active players during lesion formation and key for providing peripheral immune cells access to the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: This reference supports the statement by mentioning the role of astrocytes in providing access for peripheral immune cells to the CNS, contributing to lesion formation.

steps/12.description: Immune cells crossing the blood-brain barrier create focal areas of inflammation in the central nervous system.

evidence.snippet: This review discusses several emerging imaging technologies that could be used as surrogate markers of compartmentalized inflammation, targeting chronic active lesions, meningeal inflammation, and innate immune activation within the normal-appearing white matter and gray matter.
evidence.explanation: The deep-research review highlighted compartmentalized inflammation as a key mechanism of progression; this abstract supports the asserted lesion, meningeal, microglial/innate, and gray-matter compartments.

evidence.snippet: ELFs can be found in the meninges of around 40% of the investigated progressive multiple sclerosis (MS) post-mortem brain tissues and are associated with the severity of cortical degeneration and clinical disease progression.
evidence.explanation: Sources the meningeal compartment specifically, which the node and the canonical hypothesis both assert. Ectopic lymphoid follicles occur in roughly 40% of progressive-MS post-mortem brains and track cortical degeneration severity and clinical progression. Carry the 40% as an approximate post-mortem prevalence: the same review notes that the absence of a uniform ELF definition impedes reproducible comparison across neuropathology series.

steps/13.description: Chronic inflammation behind a relatively closed blood-brain barrier, including chronic active lesions, meningeal inflammation, and innate immune activation, contributes to smoldering tissue injury and disability progression not fully captured by conventional relapse-focused MRI outcomes.

evidence.snippet: The expression of NLRP3, IL1B, IL18, CASP1 and PYCARD transcripts were elevated in chronic active lesions (CALs) in PPMS cases, with no significant alterations determined in SPMS CNS tissue.
evidence.explanation: Primary post-mortem brain evidence localizing NLRP3 inflammasome pathway upregulation specifically to chronic active lesions in progressive MS.

evidence.snippet: NLRP3-dependent IL-1β release, alongside NLRP3, IL1B and GSDMD expression, were significantly elevated in immune cells isolated from pwMS (primarily RRMS), when compared to PBMCs from healthy controls.

evidence.snippet: the levels of autophagy and mitophagy markers are significantly increased in the biofluids of MS patients during the active phase of the disease, indicating activation of these processes

evidence.snippet: further changes in these autophagy genes were verified in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) engulfed myelin debris (MD)

evidence.snippet: Becn1 showed obvious expression abnormalities suggesting that this gene has vital functions in autophagy and MD engulfed by OPCs

steps/15.description: Autophagic and mitophagic flux is dysregulated in MS lesions: microglial autophagy declines with age and disease-associated activation, impairing phagocytic clearance of myelin debris, while autophagy and mitophagy marker levels rise in patients' biofluids during active disease and in demyelinating models, where the resulting autophagic flux itself contributes to impaired mitochondrial function and defective myelin production. The pathway's core ATG-mediated cytoplasmic quality-control function is lost either way, so this node conforms to the disabled macroautophagy hallmark-of-aging module rather than asserting a single direction of dysregulation.

evidence.snippet: P16+ cell counts were significantly increased in WMLs and GMLs, compared with NAWM, CWM, NAGM, and CGM and lipofuscin+ cells were significantly increased in WMLs, compared with NAWM and CWM, indicating more abundant CS in demyelinated lesions.

evidence.snippet: we observed an accelerated epigenetic aging of the myelinated, normal appearing white matter of multiple sclerosis (MS) patients compared to healthy individuals

steps/16.description: p16INK4a+ and 53BP1+ senescent cells accumulate within actively demyelinating white- and gray-matter lesions, with co-localization to oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia, macrophages, and neurons. Senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors are elevated in the CSF of affected patients, and a higher senescent-cell burden is associated with faster disability progression. Inflammation-induced senescence markers can also be induced in human oligodendrocyte-lineage cells directly by pro-inflammatory microglial secretions.

evidence.snippet: Multiple structurally and mechanistically unrelated inhibitors of autophagy improved myelin production and normalized axonal myelination

evidence.snippet: P16+ cell counts in WMLs exhibited an inverse correlation with time to requiring a wheelchair and with age at death.

edges/16.description: NLRP3-dependent IL-1beta/IL-18 maturation and gasdermin-D-associated pyroptotic signaling within chronic active lesions add a further, innate-immune route to the tissue injury that manifests as axonal damage.

evidence.snippet: By analyzing 8,711 individuals, we showed that heterozygote carriers of this low-frequency variant have an increased risk of vitamin D insufficiency... Individuals carrying one copy of this variant also had increased odds of multiple sclerosis...

evidence.snippet: Overall, the results of these studies support a protective effect of vitamin D, but there are uncertainties and many unanswered questions, including how vitamin D exerts a protective effect, how genetic variations modify the effect, and whether vitamin D can influence the course of MS progression.

edges/17.description: Graded below the Epstein-Barr link into this same node. The second item is the more interesting of the two and the reason this link is drawn at all: a low-frequency coding variant that raises the risk of vitamin D insufficiency also raises the odds of this disease, which is a genetic-instrument argument rather than another observational association. evidence.snippet: The strongest known risk factor for MS is infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). evidence.snippet: MS does not develop in the absence of EBV exposure, and EBV is necessary, but insufficient on its own, to cause disease.
evidence.explanation: States that the disease does not develop in the absence of this exposure and that the virus is necessary but insufficient alone. A necessity claim, from a model-organism thesis, so it is carried at partial and not alone.

edges/18.description: Graded above the vitamin D link into this same node, on evidence rather than on preference: this exposure has a quantified hazard, is described by its source as the strongest known risk factor for the disease, and is argued elsewhere to be necessary though not sufficient. The intermediates are nonetheless unknown, because no cited sentence follows the virus to myelin-reactive T cells; the route from infection to this node is exactly what the field is still arguing about.

evidence.snippet: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is considered a prototype inflammatory autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system (CNS)

evidence.snippet: Serum levels of neurofilament light chain, a biomarker of neuroaxonal degeneration, increased only after EBV seroconversion.
evidence.explanation: Supports the ordering the notes assert, not just the association: in the >10 million-person military cohort the neuroaxonal-degeneration biomarker rose only after EBV seroconversion, placing the exposure upstream of measurable CNS injury. Surfaced by the 2026 OpenScientist run; the notes above had named this cohort without citing it.

evidence.snippet: In all phenotypes, PIRA represented the main disability accrual mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the PIRA qualification in the notes above.
